speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege, affecting not only myself but every member of this house. On January 21 the hon. member
for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) raised a similar question. No answer, so far as I know, has been forthcoming from the government and I desire to demonstrate that the practice of which he complained is still continuing and to register my firmest and most emphatic protest against it.
I hold in my hand an air mail envelope postmarked "Wolfville, N.S."-which is in the constituency of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley)-"February 12, 1942." The end of this envelope has a label pasted over it, upon which appear the following words: "Examined by DB/C 106." This label obscures any initials which may have appeared on the envelope, but the following appears very clearly, "Hanson, Esq., M.P., Leader of the Opposition, Parliament Buildings, Ottawa, Ont." There could have been no doubt in the mind of the censor that this letter was addressed to me as a member of parliament and as leader of the opposition. The censor none the less took upon himself to open and examine this letter.
I protest, first of all, against that. In this connection I should like to draw the attention of the house to the reply made by the Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock) to the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) on January 21 last, Hansard, page 4463, in which the hon. member asked this question:
If any criticism of a department of government has been found, has such criticism been extracted from letters and sent with the name of the writer to the department involved?
The answer of the Postmaster General was:
Such extracts are referred in confidence to the head of the department concerned, when it is considered in the public interest to do so.
In other words, if this letter from the constituency of the Minister of Finance, addressed to me as a member of parliament and as leader of the opposition, had contained critical reference to the minister's conduct of his department, shall I say, it might have been referred to the minister.
Mr. Speaker, this is an intolerable situation and one which the members of this house cannot permit to continue. This practice converts a censorship, which exists solely for the purpose of securing the safety of the state in wartime, into a petty Gestapo spying upon members of parliament and others.
May I make it very clear that my protest is not based upon any objection to the contents of this particular letter being made known to anyone. I hold it in my hand and anybody who wants to do so can read it. The letter is merely a general condemnation of the plebiscite and I would have no hesitation in reading it to the house if anybody wants to hear it. My protest is based upon a principle and that principle I enunciate
592	COMMONS
Privilege-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
as follows: Mail addressed to any member of parliament or dispatched by any member of parliament must be considered inviolate and free from interference by any servant of the crown. Unless this principle is firmly established, I do not believe it is possible for members of parliament adequately to perform their duties. If it is possible, as it is, for a letter addressed by me to, shall I say, the leader of the Conservative party in Nova Scotia, or by such leader to me, to be examined by a censor and the contents thereof communicated to the Postmaster General or even to the Prime Minister himself, I do not see how anyone can continue to carry on the duties of leader of the opposition. I do not say that this has occurred, but, under the procedure followed, it may occur.
I propose to lay on the table of the house the envelope to which I have referred. I protest against this practice with all the vigour and emphasis at my command and I ask the house to deal with this violation of privilege. Unless I have an unequivocal assurance that this practice will be stopped immediately I shall take the earliest opportunity to assert by way of a motion the rights and privileges of members of this parliament.
Mr. Speaker, I am trying to carry on one of the functions of government-perhaps in an inadequate manner but nevertheless with all the loyalty and power at my command- but if I am to be subject to this sort of espionage, I shall protest to the utmost and if I get no redress I shall carry the matter to the court of public opinion.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: May I say first, with respect to the underlying principles that are vital in the matter to which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has just referred, that I am in entire agreement with him. May I also say that if what I have been told is correct, some of my own mail has been similarly opened by censors, against which I wish to protest just as strongly as he has done.

maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I am in good company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: It could not be better for either of us. May I say further something with which I am sure my hon. friend will be the first to agree. It is that great difficulties present themselves to some of the officials who are discharging public duties, in the matter of carrying out the instructions given to them. The letter to which my hon. friend has referred, as well as that referred to the other day, were air-mail letters, if I am not mistaken?

maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: And there is the further fact, I believe, that they came from areas known for certain military reasons as prohibited defence areas. I think there is a part of the district represented by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) which is a prohibited area.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Halifax is, but I did not think any part of my constituency is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I understand that part of Halifax is. I cannot say just how far the area extends, but there are certain prohibited defence areas and certain restrictions in regard to air mail coming from those areas. I should not be surpised if that and that alone is the reason for the opening of the letter of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition.
I can assure him that the last thing any member of the administration would wish is to have his mail or the mail of any hon. member opened for purposes of espionage or anything of the kind. I shall take up at once with the ministers concerned with censorship the representations which have been made, and see if it is not possible to have any occurrence of this kind prevented in the future. Hon. members will realize that in a time of war of necessity there are occasions when with the utmost desire to give the fullest discretion to officials they may err. on what they regard as the side of strict compliance with instructions. I am sure the present instance is one of that kind only.

maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I should like to add this: I realize that from a proclaimed defence area such as Halifax a good deal more care has to be taken than from an area which is not a defence area. But Wolf-ville is not a defence area. An air mail letter is mailed at Wolfville; I assume it goes to Halifax and takes the plane there. But it does not originate in Halifax. I think we ought to know what instructions are given to the censors. A letter directed by a citizen of this country to a member of parliament should not be opened even if it does take the plane at Halifax. I should like to know what the rules are.
In the early part of the war I was in Florida, and my family was living at Halifax, and all our mail was censored. I expected that; there was the element, an important one, of possible contravention of the regulations of the foreign exchange control board. Such mail was international in character. People have sought to send securities out of the country by mail, and the foreign exchange control board exercise some control over that through the censorship. That is quite proper. But mail from Wolfville to Ottawa surely should

never be opened. I cannot see on what principle they are opened. I suppose it is charitable to think that probably it is due to some too officious official. But that is not enough; we ought to know what the rules are.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I shall try to get for my hon. friend the information he has requested. I would only wish to substitute the word "conscientious" for "officious".

maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Well, I think it is officious.

maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: May I add a word in this connection, as I happened to bring this subject to the attention of the Postmaster General? The Prime Minister has said that he thought this opening of letters by the censors would apply only to air mail letters. In one case a letter was opened, an ordinary letter, mailed to my wife from Montreal. It happened to contain a Christmas card. It seems extraordinary that that should happen. I have been informed that on other occasions photostatic copies have been made of extracts from letters and these have been sent to the departments of government concerned when there has been criticism.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I think the last statement of my hon. friend is one on which the government should have a little more information. If he can advise me of any instance in which photostatic prints have been made from letters and sent to the government, I should like to have particulars.

maintopic: CENSORSHIP OF MAIL ADDRESSED TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: The Postmaster General said it was done.

maintopic: THE WAR IN THE FAR EAST
THE WAR IN THE FAR EAST
subtopic: FALL OF SINGAPORE-TRIBUTE TO HEROIC RESISTANCE OF ITS DEFENDERS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE WAR IN THE FAR EAST
subtopic: FALL OF SINGAPORE-TRIBUTE TO HEROIC RESISTANCE OF ITS DEFENDERS
speechtext:
Hon. members will I assume be anxious to know whether the government has received any information with regard to the critical situation in the far east which it is in a position to impart, beyond the momentous announcement made yesterday by the prime minister of Great Britain (Mr. Churchill) in the course of his world-wide broadcast that Singapore has fallen. Hon. members will I am sure appreciate the fact that such information as our government receives with respect to matters in the far east comes to us for the most part from London. There are very few connections between Canada and the far east if we except
the direct communications we have with Australia and New Zealand. So far as London itself is concerned the sources that may be regarded as reliable with respect to events and happenings in the far east are becoming increasingly limited, and in Britain the government itself is obliged to take additional precautions by way of investigating the reliability of information before sending it out.
We have thus far received no information that would throw additional light upon the situation in the far east, beyond the announcement that was made by the Prime Minister yesterday.
I am sure, however, that hon. members would not wish this fateful hour to pass without some recognition on the part of the parliament and the people of Canada of the heroic resistance of the defenders of Singapore, a resistance which will be recalled throughout time as comparable to any recorded chapter of valour and endurance. The position of the defenders of Singapore has deeply stirred the hearts of the Canadian people. It has made us more determined than ever to resist with all our might onslaughts of the enemy where-ever we can assist to that end, and to devote the utmost of our strength to the defence of freedom. This major reverse should not be allowed to become an excuse for undue pessimism, or undue recriminations. I should like to re-echo the words of the Prime Minister of Great Britain that as a people we must steel ourselves against "many misfortunes, severe and torturing losses, remorseless and gnawing anxieties." At the same time we must, with a faith that is stronger than ever, believe, again to quote Mr. Churchill, that the same qualities which brought the British people through the awful jeopardy of the summer of 1940 will bring all through this new ordeal.
Let me add, too, that with the Prime Minister of Great Britain I believe nothing could be more harmful at the present or any time than a lack of unity within our nation, or between the nations that to-day are united in seeking to preserve the liberties of mankind. We must stand together as never before in preserving our national unity and the unity of the united nations. For Canada the fall of Singapore should emphasize the gravity of the whole world situation. Coming, on the eve of the victory loan campaign, it should serve to bring forth from the people of Canada a full and immediate response to the loan as an essential factor in the war effort of our country.
Secret Session

subtopic: REQUEST FOR OPPORTUNITY TO DISCUSS DEFENCE MEASURES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR OPPORTUNITY TO DISCUSS DEFENCE MEASURES
speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) whether any decision has been reached by the government concerning the suggestion that there should be a secret session of the house to consider the question of the defence of the Pacific coast, or of both coasts. The fall of Singapore may mean that Canada has only a limited time in which to prepare.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REQUEST FOR OPPORTUNITY TO DISCUSS DEFENCE MEASURES
speechtext: The government has had in mind the suggestion advanced that a secret session of the house should be held. Thus far we have had the intention of holding that session at a date which, all factors considered, we believed would be most advisable. We had felt that the debate on the address should be concluded before a secret session was held, unless there were some special reason to the contrary. We have also felt that if the plebiscite bill could be passed and sent to the other house as speedily as possible, that would be desirable. We would then make the plebiscite the next measure to be considered, and immediately thereafter have the secret session which has been requested. If, however, there should be a general feeling that it would be desirable to have a secret session earlier than that, the government will seek to meet that desire. 1 am inclined to believe that if the secret session could be held at about the time I have indicated it would perhaps serve the purpose my hon. friends have in view.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR OPPORTUNITY TO DISCUSS DEFENCE MEASURES
speechtext: May I suggest to the Prime Minister that time is precious these days, and that he consider whether or not the secret session should be held before the plebiscite bill is under discussion, because that discussion may last for some time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REQUEST FOR OPPORTUNITY TO DISCUSS DEFENCE MEASURES
speechtext: Of course it is the emphasis that has been placed upon time being precious that makes us wish to get the plebiscite bill through as soon as possible. My colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) mentions to me that members of the staff of his department have certain steps in view which might obviate the necessity of having an immediate discussion on the Pacific situation. He feels that matters might be put in such shape that the house might be more fully informed if the steps that are now being taken could be taken before the secret session is held.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR OPPORTUNITY TO DISCUSS DEFENCE MEASURES
speechtext: I rose to say something similar, except that I think the secret session should be held immediately, and that even this debate should be suspended in view of the general situation which is developing. And I do not believe any secret session should be concerned only with Pacific coast defences. It should deal with the whole of our defence effort and with our production; that is to say, there should be a complete inquiry into the situation as it now exists. Members of this house know very little more than the general public. It is about time we assumed our responsibilities and went into this thing very thoroughly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: REQUEST FOR OPPORTUNITY TO DISCUSS DEFENCE MEASURES
speechtext: May I say to my hon. friend, the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, that if the feeling is as he has expressed it, namely that the secret session should be held immediately, then we might agree at once to have the session held as soon as the debate on the address has been concluded. I believe there is a general understanding that this may take place to-morrow night.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition) :
subtopic: REQUEST FOR OPPORTUNITY TO DISCUSS DEFENCE MEASURES
speechtext: I think we should get this debate concluded, and then we might get together and decide on a date for a secret session and what should be discussed. I am afraid that if we undertook in secret session to cover the whole gamut of government operations and responsibilities we would have a debate lasting as long as this debate on the address. I think it is a matter on which we might get together and perhaps evolve a programme; I believe that would1 be a fair suggestion to make.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR OPPORTUNITY TO DISCUSS DEFENCE MEASURES
speechtext: May I say that the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver South Mr. Green) with respect to a secret session to discuss defence on the Pacific coast might lead one to think that we on the Atlantic coast have not the same feelings about our defence as the people on the Pacific coast. I urge that at any secret session of the house where the question of defence on the Pacific coast is taken up, the government be prepared to discuss as of equal importance and equal urgency the question of defence on the Atlantic coast.

subtopic: PRESS REPORT OF STATEMENT OF PREMIER OF ONTARIO AS TO DISCHARGES BECAUSE OF LACK OF PROPER CLOTHING

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. IAN A. MACKENZIE (Minister of Pensions and National Health): My attention has deen directed to a dispatch appearing in the Toronto Globe and Mail of Friday, February 13, containing a statement attributed to the premier of Ontario, as follows:
"He said 45,000 men had been discharged from the armed forces mostly because they developed colds and tuberculosis from lack of proper clothing."
Every implication of this grossly alarmist statement is totally unjustified. Out of more than 400,000 enlistments up to the end of December the total number discharged as medically unfit was only 27,153. The number
45,000	represents the number struck off the strength for all reasons, including among others the following: misconduct; false attestation; over and under age; compassionate grounds; unlikely to become efficient soldiers; returned to civil employment in which they had special skill. The number discharged as medically unfit, I repeat, was 27,153, which is approximately 6-75 per cent of enlistments.
A statistical analysis of the conditions leading to discharge is complete with respect to
21,000	cases dealt with prior to November 1. To suggest that tuberculosis is a major condition is utterly and entirely untrue. Up to the first of the year the number of the members of the forces discharged for physical unfitness, including wounds, was less than 7 per cent of total enlistments. For more detailed statistics, I have to go back to November 1.
Since the outbreak of war it has been an automatic procedure that the file of every member of the forces discharged as medically unfit shall be referred immediately to the Canadian pension commission for a ruling. The number of cases upon which rulings had been given on November 1 amounted to 20,982. The number of cases of tuberculosis among these were 1,320. At that time the number of enlistments in all three services was around
360,000.
The total number of cases of tuberculosis was, therefore, only one-third of one per cent of the whole of our Canadian forces in the present war. This figure includes a very large number of non-active cases-that is, of men who were found to have spots on their lungs, which made it unwise for them to continue in military service for fear of some later breakdown, but who at the time were quite well and able to carry on in ordinary civil life.
Every man enlisting in the Canadian forces in this war is given a careful X-ray examination for the purpose of detecting chest conditions which may escape attention at tlie ordinary clinical examination.

subtopic: PRESS REPORT OF STATEMENT OF PREMIER OF ONTARIO AS TO DISCHARGES BECAUSE OF LACK OF PROPER CLOTHING
speechtext: When did that practice begin?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PRESS REPORT OF STATEMENT OF PREMIER OF ONTARIO AS TO DISCHARGES BECAUSE OF LACK OF PROPER CLOTHING
speechtext: I am just going to refer to that. Ip the early months of the war this X-ray was not taken until perhaps three or four months after enlistment.

subtopic: PRESS REPORT OF STATEMENT OF PREMIER OF ONTARIO AS TO DISCHARGES BECAUSE OF LACK OF PROPER CLOTHING
speechtext: Right.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PRESS REPORT OF STATEMENT OF PREMIER OF ONTARIO AS TO DISCHARGES BECAUSE OF LACK OF PROPER CLOTHING
speechtext:
Now, in most cases, it is taken at the time of enlistment, often before attestation has been completed. The Canadian Tuberculosis Association has kept a careful record of the results of these X-ray examinations and I am advised that of all the cases of tuberculosis detected in these examinations only 40 per cent were active. The remainder were inactive or quiescent.
The vast majority of these non-active cases were detected within a very short time after enlistment, indicating (1) that the condition had arisen prior to enlistment, (2) that it had
596	COMMONS
Armed Forces-Lack of Proper Clothing
not been aggravated by the man's short experience in the army, and (3) that -the precautions taken by the government have probably saved young men's lives; since a man with this weakness, if subjected to the rigours of military life for a prolonged period, would undoubtedly break down.
The foregoing figures clearly indicate that of the small number of cases of tuberculosis detected in the armed forces, the vast majority existed before enlistment. Our law provides that if a condition such as tuberculosis is found to have been caused by service, or to have been aggravated by service, the man is pensionable. I have already shown that among the 21,000 men discharged as physically unfit prior to November 1, the Canadian Pension commission had found 1,320 cases of tuberculosis. These cases include the men who have been attested for only a few days, and then discharged. The extent to which tuberculosis has been caused by or aggravated by military service is reflected in the number of pension awards made. That number, up to November 1, was 39-for tuberculosis, in all our forces. That is, out of 360,000 men enlisted by November 1, we have the following facts:
Fewer than 7 per cent were discharged as physically unfit, and this 7 per cent includes a large number in whom weaknesses of preenlistment origin were detected by X-ray within a few days or weeks of enlistment. It includes only 1,320 cases of tuberculosis, the vast majority of which were non-active. The tqtal number of cases of tuberculosis found in the armed forces represents only one-third of one per cent of the men enlisted. The number of tuberculosis cases due to, or aggravated by service, was 39, all told-a number too small to be expressed in any percentage figures.
The fact that we have 1,320 cases of tuberculosis recorded indicates not that the provision for the health of the troops is inadequate, but that the efficiency of our medical services has saved a large number of men with lung weaknesses from undergoing the rigours of military training.
Instead of conditions in the armed services having brought about large numbers of cases of tuberculosis, as so recklessly implied by the premier of Ontario, the efficiency of our medical examinations has actually saved hundreds of lives, and revealed to many young civilians the existence of unsuspected lung weaknesses, which they can now intelligently protect.
The irresponsible and unfounded statement by the premier of Ontario may have several consequences. First, it may needlessly alarm tens of thousands of mothers and wives as to

the care their boys are receiving in the armed services of Canada. Such a statement is therefore entirely improper and thoroughly indefensible. Second, it may give comfort to the enemy by belittling the efficiency of our fighting forces. There is only one word in the English language to describe such conduct- and I shall not use it here. In the third place it may shake public confidence in the government of our country. That, of course, the premier of Ontario regards as fair game in these grim, dark days of war, as well as in the more pleasant days of peace.
I leave this whole unhappy affair to two tribunals, one being indefinite and uncertain, the elastic conscience of the man who pronounced the libel, the other very definite and certain and purposeful, the free and unfettered judgment of hon. members of this house. In my own opinion the statement was thoroughly contemptible.

speechtext: Will the minister consider using paragraph 39 (b) of the defence of Canada regulations empowering the government to intern any person making statements likely to interfere with recruiting?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: PRESS REPORT OF STATEMENT OF PREMIER OF ONTARIO AS TO DISCHARGES BECAUSE OF LACK OF PROPER CLOTHING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following what my colleague has said, I should like to place on record the figures for the Canadian army. It will be remembered that Premier Hepburn's statement was that 45,000 men had been discharged from the armed1 forces, mostly because they had developed colds and tuberculosis because of lack of proper clothing.
As I understand it, the 45,000 is a rough figure arrived at for all discharges from all causes. The number found medically unfit after they enlisted in the army was 29,476. That is the number for two and a third years, stretching from September 1, 1939 to December 31, 1941. That is, 29,476 of those who had enlisted were subsequently found medically unfit.
Premier Hepburn's statement is that the discharges were "mostly because they developed' colds and tuberculosis from lack of proper clothing". Of the 29,476 found unfit, only 1,499, or 5-1 per cent, were found unfit on account of tuberculosis. And only 55 of these men who were found unfit from this cause were so found after they had gone overseas. That is to say, there were 55 cases of discharge for tuberculosis, out of over
130.000	men overseas. It should be remembered also that the total of 1,499 men who were found unfit on account of tuberculosis is out of an aggregate enlistment in the Canadian army for this same period of nearly
300.000	men.

Hong Kong Atrocities
Premier Hepburn also includes colds as reasons for discharge. I think it ought to be known that ordinary colds are not a cause for discharge. Discharges are made where there is a chronic or serious cause of affection of the respiratory system, such as in the case of asthma, bronchitis and things of that kind. I have had these looked up as well. The total number of men who have enlisted in the army and who have later been found unfit on account of an affection of the respiratory system is 3,015 out of total found unfit of 29,476, or 10-2 per cent. Again, this number of 3,015 is out of a total enlistment of nearly
300,000.
To sum up, Premier Hepburn says that "45,000 men had been discharged from the armed forces mostly because they developed colds and tuberculosis from lack of proper clothing." The facts are that out of 29,476 found medically unfit after enlistment, only 5-1 per cent were found medically unfit on account of tuberculosis-as a matter of fact, about 40 per cent of those were non-active. And about ten per cent of those found medically unfit were cases of affection of the respiratory system. In other words, taking the total number discharged for tuberculosis, asthma, bronchitis or any other disease of the respiratory system, which might include chronic or serious colds, the total discharges were 4,514 out of 29,476, or a little over 15 per cent of those actually found unfit, and that 4,514 was out of a total number actually enlisted of nearly 300,000.
I think these facts speak for themselves without any embellishment from me.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. G. POWER (Minister of National Defence for Air):
speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PRESS REPORT OF STATEMENT OF PREMIER OF ONTARIO AS TO DISCHARGES BECAUSE OF LACK OF PROPER CLOTHING
speechtext:
With respect to the Royal Canadian Air Force, I have before me an itemized list of discharges and retirements for medical reasons, September, 1939, to January 31, 1942. I would point out that discharges for medical reasons only total 2,270. Discharges for tuberculosis total 136, and for respiratory diseases, as explained by my hon. friend the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), 141.
Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Mr. Speaker, to complete the story with regard to discharges from the armed forces, I should like to say that so far as the Royal Canadian Navy is concerned the total number of discharges for medical reasons from the beginning of the war up to January 31, 1942, was 954. Of that number 53 discharges were because of tuberculosis and 56 were for other diseases of the respiratory system.

subtopic: PRESS REPORTS AS TO ATROCITIES UPON CAPTURED CANADIAN TROOPS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PRESS REPORTS AS TO ATROCITIES UPON CAPTURED CANADIAN TROOPS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister based upon two news items, one of which appeared on page 3 of the Ottawa Citizen of February 13 and the other on the front page of the Ottawa Citizen of this morning. These articles describe barbarities and atrocities that are alleged to have been perpetrated upon Canadian troops captured in Hong Kong. The latter dispatch carried a footnote to the effect that the Department of External Affairs is taking immediate action to check the truthfulness of these reports. In the meantime I hope that the public of Canada will not assume as reliable, communications that are not authenticated by the government itself.

speechtext:
I should like to reply to a 
question asked by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) with respect to Canadian representation on the Pacific council. This question was asked on February 10 and the hon. member's remarks will be found on pages 444 and 445 of Hansard:
The Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, in a speech in the. House of Commons at Westminster on January 27, which was quoted in this house in reply to a question from the member from Vancouver South (Mr. Green) on the following day, announced that it was proposed to set up in London a Pacific council, comprising Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand and the Netherlands, which would be able to transmit their united views to the combined chiefs of staff committee sitting at Washington. Definite arrangements had not at that time been made for the establishment and location of the council and, as members of the house will be aware, suggestions were put forward in certain quarters that it should meet in Washington rather than in London. It has now been settled that it will meet in London, and the following official announcement of its constitution has been made public:
A Pacific council has been set up on a ministerial plane. Australia, Great Britain, the Netherlands and New Zealand will have representation on the council. Other ministers and advisers will attend as necessary.
At the first meeting of the council, held on February 10, the government of India was represented in addition to the governments named in the official announcement.
Since the question of Canadian representation in the Pacific council was raised in this house I have been again in communication with the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom on the matter. The council's functions and responsibility are not quite as wide as its name might suggest. The Prime Minister has stressed the fact that as present constituted its duties are directly related to questions of regional defence of the areas in the southwest Pacific and southeastern Asia against which Japanese offensive action is now directed. The countries participating in it are those actually in the zone of hostilities.
It may be, however, that future strategic requirements will make it desirable to .enlarge the scope of the Pacific council to include the whole Pacific area, in which case Canada will certainly be represented on the council.

Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday last the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) asked on the orders of the day whether it was the intention of the government to make the report of the last interprovincial conference available to all members of parliament and "if so, will it be an unrevised copy".

The meeting, however, agreed that the record should be confidential, and I think hon. members will understand that in a meeting of this sort between governments in which certain aspects of the financial affairs and position of the various governments were discussed, freedom of discussion would have been seriously impeded if any other decision had been reached. It is, therefore, not the intention of the government to -table the "report" of the meeting or make it public in any other way, although as the house is
aware, I have already tabled copies of the tentative draft agreements which were, if I may put it this way, the basis and the result of our discussions.
The hon. member also asked whether any member of the government informed the provincial representatives attending this conference that there were Canadian soldiers, sailors and airmen at Singapore as well as at Hong Kong. As I have already explained, the meeting was for the purpose of discussing tax matters arising out of the offer made to the provinces in the last dominion budget and' no reference was made by myself or, to my knowledge, by any other member of the government to members of the Canadian armed forces serving at Singapore or anywhere else.

speechtext:
of the speech from the throne which dealt with the proposed plebiscite. If that were the sole matter I proposed to discuss I doubt very much if I would have taken part in this debate to-day. The very excellent contributions to the debate made by the mover (Mr. Fournier) and the seconder (Mr. Macdonald) of the address in reply, the statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and by other ministers and the many able contributions made by other members of the house, seem to me to have reasonably served the purpose of the debate and there is very little of value left for me to say. However, having in mind that I propose to speak on another phase of the speech from the throne, I decided that if I remained silent my attitude might be misinterpreted- as in opposition or at least lukewarmness to the policy of the government. Such a supposition would be wholly incorrect. I can say, as one member said, that both my mind and my conscience are in agreement in supporting the government in the matter of the plebiscite. I consider that the Prime Minister oould do no other than he has done in observing the pledge he gave the people of Canada in the election of 1940. Once you accept that premise, it seems to me there is only one alternative to the plebiscite, and that would be a general election. I believe we would all be in agreement, both in this house and outside, that in the present crisis that course is one that no one would wisely or properly consider. Moreover, ever since this government has been elected, and since I have had the privilege of being a member of this house, I have followed with all the attention I could the policies adopted, and 1 think that the war leadership displayed by the Prime Minister and his colleagues has been magnificent, to borrow a word used by a much more eminent person than myself, Mr. Churchill. I am assisted in coming to that conclusion by the statement that was made to the Canadian troops, in England by General McNaughton, the commander of our Canadian forces, a man who possesses the confidence of every section of the Canadian people, and, may I suggest, of every party in this house. It is true that General McNaughton in the position he holds might not comment at all upon the war programme of this country; but I think the fact that he did not remain silent but saw fit to give expression to his own views on the men, munitions and food that were going from Canada to England, is indeed, coming from one who is in the best position to know and to pass judgment on our war effort, a very warm recommendation for the Prime Minister and the cabinet.

Personally, after listening to the statement given by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) as to the success of the voluntary recruiting method, and having the assurance that neither at present nor in the near forseeable future will the system of voluntary recruiting occasion any shortcomings in our war effort, I think it would be unwise and inadvisable at this moment to attempt to put into operation the conscription of man-power for overseas service. I realize of course that it is wise for this government, while there is yet time, and in the light of the terrible events elsewhere, to secure from the people to whom they gave the pledge a complete release, so that under any circumstances and in any event their freedom of action to advise this parliament of the course that should be pursued shall be untrammelled and unfettered.
In my opinion, therefore, not only was it right for the Prime Minister to keep his pledge, but the method adopted of submitting to the people by way of a plebiscite the question which it is proposed to submit to them, is the wisest and best under all the circumstances. So far as the plebiscite is concerned, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, the conscription of man-power for overseas service is not an issue. I propose therefore to reserve to myself the right to discuss when the time comes, if it ever does come, the question of conscription for overseas service, and only when that question is properly before the house and becomes a matter which parliament is called upon to decide.
The subject that prompted me to take part in this debate arises out of a much more important section of the speech from the throne than that dealing with the plebiscite, because after all the plebiscite is merely a method of procedure. The part of the speech from the throne which I propose to read to the house is a part which actually deals with the attitude of the government to our war effort. Let me read that paragraph:
In accordance with the government's policy of a total national effort for total war, you will he asked to approve a balanced programme for further increases in the armed forces and in the production of munitions of war and of foodstuffs.
I wish to call the attention of the house particularly to that word "balanced". I think it is most essential to apply it to our war effort. I should like also in that connection to call the attention of the house to a sentence from the speech made by the Minister of National Defence the other day in the house, in which he said at page 448.
Total war requires a country to plan its pattern for war according to its resources, and,

The Address-Mr. Graham
more than that, according to the needs and abilities of other countries with which it is allied.
That, too, is a statement of significance, indicating the duty we have to discharge in the direction of the war effort of Canada. We should never let it escape our attention. The portion of that particular section of the speech from the throne which I wish to discuss to-day is that dealing with our programme in the production and supply of foodstuffs. I am convinced that the events of the last few weeks make it necessary for this government and for us all to completely resurvey and reappraise the position of Canada in its relationship with the United States, particularly in this matter of the production and supply of foodstuffs.
What is the situation? I think I can briefly review it, and this may be of some value to the house. It will be recalled that soon after the outbreak of war the part of Europe that had supplied great quantities of foodstuffs to Great Britain was closed to her. I need only point to Denmark, Norway, Holland, Belgium, the Danube basin, and other Eurpoean countries, which had all played their part in supplying Great Britain with the foodstuffs that were so solely needed. It is true that even after that disaster, after these sources of supply had been cut off, there was still a considerable portion of the world available to supply that vital war necessity-food. But the events of the last few weeks have completely changed that picture. Singapore has fallen, the Malay peninsula is gone, and no' one in this house can be blind to the possibilities that may flow from the victories of Japan in the far east.
What does it mean in actual terms of foodstuffs? For example, the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) has often informed this house of the great quantities of edible oil that had been furnished to Canada from that area. The United States, too, commensurately with its population, imported large quantities of that commodity; and because of her peculiar position, England, in proportion to her population, imported from that source quantities out of all ratio to those imported by the United States and Canada. Is it not clear also, now that Singapore has fallen, that the sea routes to and from Australia, New Zealand and even India, may be denied to the ships of Britain and her allies? What effect must that have in the necessity of taking care of the food problem of Britain? It seems to me it can have only one effect, that is, to place upon Canada and the United States and the other American nations which are able and willing to assume it the task of making up this tremendous deficiency in food supply resulting from the events of the last few weeks. We would be blind indeed if we did not recognize the immediate necessity of reshaping our food
policy to take care of the additional needs of our allies arising out of the situation in the far east.
It seems to me that despite the difficulty of keeping the Atlantic sea lanes open, Canada and the United States are the only countries that can possibly take up the slack caused by Britain being cut off from those countries as sources of supply. Keeping that route open will be a most difficult task, but it would appear to be the only continuous sea lane that we can hope to maintain. Australia and New Zealand, as everyone knows, have supplied great quantities of wheat, beef, mutton, butter, cheese and, as a by-product of the food supply, wool, to Great Britain, Canada and the United States.
I would point out that not only must we make up the deficiency in the supply to Britain and our own armed forces and the armed forces of our allies there, but it will be necessary to make up the deficiency that we ourselves shall feel as a result of the cutting off of those things that formerly came from the far east.
We should also have in mind that not only may it be necessary lor us to take care of Britain's needs, but it may be our task to get great quantities of food to Russia and China. Both those nations are vital partners with us in this war, and if they for a moment fail through lack of food and any share of the responsibility of that were upon the shoulders of the Canadian people, we should deeply regret our failure to take due steps in due time. It is also necessary to keep in mind that in the production of either cereals or food in the shape of live stock it takes considerable time to produce a greatly increased supply. A crop of cereals cannot be grown in less than a season, and the same applies still more in regard to live stock. The growing in Canada of soya beans, which would immediately come to our mind to replace some of the edible oils, is not very feasible. But we know that in the United States there are considerable areas where that commodity has been successfully grown. It seems to me there must be further cooperation between the United States and Canada, after consultation and consideration of the joint problem, to see to it that those areas are used for that purpose. Canada can also assist indirectly by encouraging a great increase in the growth of flax. Flax produces linseed oil. We are using considerable quantities of edible oils for non-edible purposes, and we could make up that deficiency to some extent at least by producing more linseed oil.
I have already pointed out that as I see the problem it requires the closest cooperation between United States and Canada. That
The Address-Mr. Graham

cooperation exists in many fields and it should immediately be taken into account in this very vital section of our war effort. The policy adopted by this government at the present time will of necessity have to encourage the production of the foodstuffs that we most need. In the policy to be adopted this year any suggestion of encouraging the keeping of suitable agricultural land out of production should be completely eliminated.
The situation is so serious that any land properly capable of producing any form of food should be utilized to the full, in the face of the great danger that confronts us. I used the words "suitable agricultural land". I know the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) through his long experience will have in mind the history of the last war and the difficulties that arose through encouraging the bringing into production of vast areas of western lands that were not suited to agricultural use. We should not repeat that mistake, except under the urge of dire necessity. This year certainly the policy should be to encourage the full use for production of all land that is in shape to be used. I would point out that sooner than I or probably any lion, member of this house expected the Minister of Agriculture has been proven right in two statements he made to this house. It will be recalled that he said that what we thought to be a huge surplus of wheat would in the end prove to be not a liability but a great asset. And in 1941 he told us, in introducing the wheat policy of that year, that the wheat policy would necessarily have to be a temporary one. The events to which I have referred make it quite clear that he was correct in both those statements.
I propose to deal with the question of the wheat policy, not because I believe it is not now once more in its proper alignment with the production of other foodstuffs as a national necessity, but simply because up until now wheat, it might be said, has been treated as the orphan in the storm. I think that attitude of mind on the part of the government and ourselves must cease; we must recognize that if there are areas in this country suited only to the production of wheat, they should be used for that production. It would be far better that either our allies or ourselves should have ample food supplies in the form of wheat plus a reasonable amount of fat than to find ourselves and our allies with only a little wheat and a little fat. Every acre of suitable and properly cultivated agricultural land should now be devoted to building up reserves of foodstuffs for the inevitable day when they will be needed.

Every hon. member will recall the recent visit of the four hundred farmers and others to Ottawa from Saskatchewan. I think I can safely say that they made an excellent impression on this house and, in the presentation of their submissions, on the government. Despite the criticism that was directed at the expense involved in that delegation coming to Ottawa, it is my considered opinion that they did a good job and any expenditure involved was well justified. I should also like to point out that the presentation they made to the government was most reasonable and moderate; it was made with dignity and was supported by sound arguments.
Let me give briefly the main points in that submission. They urged upon the government:
1.	That an initial pay^ment of one dollar a
bushel basis No. 1 northern at Fort William be made.
2.	Deferred payment of the balance of what they described as a parity price to be made later, this price to be determined by the bureau of statistics.
3.	The continuation of the quota system of marketing, and the taking of only the amount of wheat required for domestic consumption and export during the coming crop year.
4.	The continuation and necessary amendment of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
5.	Soil conservation and the encouragement of the production of grasses to aid in that policy.
It seems to me that this submission, in the light of the events that have taken place, merits the most favourable consideration by the government in determining the wheat policy which at present is under review. Personally I want to say that in 1941 I had no hesitation in supporting the wheat policy brought down in this house by the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It served an unusually good purpose last year in my constituency, which was visited by drought conditions almost unprecedented in our history. But I am convinced that circumstances have so changed that there is no path open to us except to recognize the needs occasioned by these events and circumstances. I believe therefore we should see to it that our policy realistically appreciates the change that has taken place. I feel that for once-and I say this to every member of this house-the interests of the nation and of our war programme are fully in keeping with the encouragement of those now producing the foodstuffs that are or will be so badly needed in connection with our war effort. Therefore, not because we are in a generous mood but

The Address-Mr. Graham
because it is right and proper and because the policy is wise and sound in the light of present circumstances, I would urge the government to see to it that for once in the history of this country, the farmer, the man whom we often proclaim to be an important element in our population, should be given that measure of justice which his situation demands and deserves.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that in connection with the policy that should be pursued by this government there has been an honest difference of opinion as to the methods by which the funds taken out of the dominion treasury should be distributed among the farming class, speaking particularly of western Canada. In view of the fact that last year we had a huge surplus of wheat which apparently we did not immediately need, the course followed then was more or less justified; but in view of the circumstances that now exist I do not believe that course should be followed any longer. I do not think it would be fair to the wheat grower, or for that matter to any other producer of foodstuffs, to say at this time, "It is vital in the interests of our war effort for you to grow all the wheat you can grow, but, because of priorities in the matter of various foodstuffs, we are going to depress the price of your commodity below what would be fair and equitable, everything being considered." I think the basis of the policy should be the establishment of fair and equitable prices to all producers of foodstuffs. Then if we wish to encourage the increased production of certain most needed agricultural commodities, we should attain that objective by paying a premium on the commodities that we desire our farmers to raise.
It seems to me this is the only reasonable attitude to assume. I further submit, Mr. Speaker, that we should encourage the greater production of coarse grains and grasses, and, as I have said already, of flax; but none of these policies should be put into operation at the expense of the wheat grower. I realize that we cannot hope to have government by delegation; I would not urge upon this house that because four hundred farmers from my own province came here and submitted their views as to the agricultural policy that should be pursued this year, that in itself should be sufficient to cause this government to follow the recommendations made by this delegation. I do feel, however, that when we examine the situation as it now exists; when we find that the policy advocated by that delegation is completely in conformity with our war needs and possible future needs, then, because it is right, proper, fair and equitable, we should give effect to that submission in its
entirety. I turn particularly to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who has direction over the framing of the wheat policy of this government. I address the Minister of Agriculture who, with his great experience in the production of foodstuffs, must be a close adviser of the government in connection with the adoption of any wheat policy. I hope also that my words may reach the ears of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), because I realize that in any policy affecting any part of our national life, the Minister of Finance plays an important part.
I believe the two ministers from the west will be fully aware of the necessity of taking into account the matters I have mentioned in drawing up the wheat policy for the coming year. We all know the Minister of Finance has undertaken a task unequalled in our previous history; I am sure he must sometimes consider that there is no ceiling whatever to the amount of money he must raise in order to take care of our war needs. But in all seriousness I do suggest to him that he should not forget what the Prime Minister has already told us, that the war effort of Canada will not be restricted by financial limitations but only by the physical capacity of this country to produce. If ever there was a time when that statement should be kept in mind, it is the present. That statement should be applied in all its vigour in regard to the production of foodstuffs in this country. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that posterity will forgive him, I am sure, if we should produce a surplus of foodstuffs and find ourselves left with that surplus on our hands; but I doubt whether posterity or the members of this house or the minister himself would forgive him if in the near future we should find ourselves and our allies faced with a serious shortage of the very staff of life itself.
It is for these reasons that I urge upon the government consideration of the new conditions with which we are faced in this world struggle; the awful potentialities that present themselves and the part Canada must play, particularly in connection with the production of foodstuffs and materials of war, in close harmony and cooperation with our great neighbour to the south. I leave this with the government in the hope that appreciation of the situation now facing us, together with the need for a new survey and appraisal of the position of Canada in connection with supplying foodstuffs, will have its effect in the policy that will be announced for this year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had decided that I would not take up any of the time of the house by participating in this debate. How-
The Address-Mr. McGarry

ever, having been exposed to what might be called the infection of intermittent fever, generated by the very heated debates that have been carried on as to conscription versus the plebiscite, my powers of resistance weakened and I fell for a slight attack of the contagion. The few remarks I shall make will reflect the symptons of that mild seizure.
Before directing my attention to the subject matter of the debate I wish to associate myself with the eloquent and complimentary tributes paid the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Sound in substance, logical, factual, devoid of partisan colouring, they were veritable masterpieces, reflecting credit alike upon the hon. members who delivered them and the constituencies they represent.
Of all the items dealt with in the speech from the throne, the one which most agitated the minds of the public, the press and hon. members, was the plebiscite. Were I to presume to give a dictionary definition of the term "plebiscite", as applied generally, I would provoke the scorn of every hon. member, because I realize full well each hon. member is capable of giving that definition himself. But concerning the word plebiscite as applied in this specific instance there seems to be some difference of meaning. One would understand from some hon. members that the plebiscite as applied in this instance is a harmful thing, and that some ulterior purposes have been concealed. I fail to see why those hon. members should take that stand. My own view is that it is the most honourable, courageous and democratic means our leader could take to ask the electorate to release him from commitments made not only by himself but, with very few exceptions, by almost every other hon. member in the house.
Those who have spoken in opposition to the plebiscite have argued that it will delay our war effort. They urge that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) should peremptorily bring in a measure of conscription, and they would fain make the house and public believe that that is the only manoeuvre essential to bringing about an all-out war effort. Canada's organization for this all-out effort was well explained to the house when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) made his very excellent speech here about a week ago. I was interested to learn that Colonel 0. M. Biggar, who certainly should be recognized as an authority, agreed entirely with the order of requirements set out by the minister.
Those requirements were set out in five Basses. The first was to ensure enough service and enough supplies to maintain the physical and mental health of our population. 
The second was to provide troops to protect Canada from invasion. The third was to build as many ships and manufacture as much war equipment as our materials and facilities permit. The fourth was to send across the seas as much food and war equipment as would be required to supply the needs of our home forces, part of the British forces and part of the civilian population. The fifth, and last, was to send overseas, out of Canada, troops who would be prepared to meet and to defeat the enemy wherever found.
As Colonel Biggar pointed out, compulsory overseas service was relevant to the attainment of only one of these requirements, namely that of providing troops for overseas service. It was indicated, in fact, only for a part of one of the requirements, because, as is known, there is no lack of recruiting in our naval and air forces. All hon. members know that only a small fraction of our overseas forces have contacted the enemy. We know, too, that if troops are recruited in Canada for Canada's protection those troops can be trained here, and if the time comes when there is a change of circumstances in the process of the war, their responsibility can be altered by the voice of the Canadian people.
We must bear in mind that man-power and woman-power in Canada is limited. Nobody knows to-day how far that power can be extended, any more than do we know which of these five requirements will be the most essential. Compulsory service for overseas is applied to only one of those requirements, and that only in a limited degree. Only a small fraction of the troops mustered to-day have been utilized. In my view the delay now obtaining is a proper one; it permits the people to concentrate on the question whether or not it is proper to extend the full power to our government. For that hesitation and concentration the government is taking full responsibility.
Listening to the speeches of some hon. members opposite, and reading some press comments, one might be led to believe that the government's war effort was away below what it should be. If I may be permitted for a few moments I should like to turn over a few pages of the history of this war, and hurriedly give a brief synopsis of what the government has already done.
First of all, in this fiscal year Canada is spending more than she spent during the whole of the duration of the last war. In other words 40 per cent of our national income is being spent to-day in the war effort. Or, if we may put it in another way, we are spending at the rate of $4,000,000 a day. Five times as many people in Canada are paying

The Address-Mr. McGarry
to-day five times as much taxes, through all means of taxation. Men and women with incomes of from $3,000 to $10,000 are paying taxes increased from 4 per cent to 11 per cent. Then, 130,000 of our young men have been taught in the art of war and, since the beginning of the war, 750,000 men have been employed in connection therewith.
The British commonwealth air training plan in three years of operation has cost Canada an amount equivalent to the whole of Canada's taxation in one fiscal year. Fifteen times as many men are employed to-day in shipbuilding as were employed: before the war, and thirty-five times as many are employed in aircraft work. The total production of explosives this year in Canada will be greater than the total production during the last war. Canadian-made army vehicles are serving in every arena of war where British empire troops are participating. To-day Canada is paying more per capita to provide foodstuffs for the British empire than the British government itself is paying for the same purpose. Canada's navy has increased from 15 ships at the beginning of the war to 350 at the present time. We have an army of 265,000; our air force numbers 100,000, and we have 150,000 men serving overseas. Some of our ships are separated by 10,000 miles. They have been engaged not only in protecting our shores but in convoy duty. They have convoyed 7,000 ships overseas, carrying a total of 43,000,000 tons of cargo. The Canadian active force comprises 393,000 men, almost half of whom are serving throughout the British empire, some in England, some in the British West Indies, some in Newfoundland, and some in Gibraltar. The air training plan now has 92 schools.. Canada has built about 200,000 automotive vehicles, an average of one every three minutes. Up to date there have been manufactured in this country 9,000,000 shells, 10,000,000 cases and 150,000,000 pounds of explosives. Canada is producing every type of gun, armament or equipment used to-day in modern war.
This is a synopsis of Canada's achievement since the wTar began. But it may not be immune to criticism. It may be said that we were slow in building tanks and ships, but anyone who realizes the transpositions that were necessary to convert this country from a peaceful nation into a belligerent country will be ready to credit Canada with a wonderful achievement. Canada has a comparatively small population. Our recruiting has been satisfactory and we have a waiting list for the navy and air force. Only a small portion of our forces has been utilized, but the danger to our own shores is becoming more menacing and imminent.
I fail to see why this matter of conscription should be considered so essential to our having a balanced all-out war effort. This bogy of conscription is being urged by the press and by other people. Sometimes I am inclined to think that people who urge conscription are more concerned with bringing about disunion in this country than they are in effecting a more unified effort. God forbid that this will result in an advantage to our financial barons of Baronfield.
I consider that our leader and his government are doing a good job. They are doing first things first. They have laid particular stress upon those things which have the greatest significance. So far they have been allowed to pursue their war effort one hundred per cent, but with the passage of time it may be necessary to have their power extended. They are asking the people in an honourable, courageous and democratic way to relieve them from the restrictions of their commitments so that when the time comes they will have a free hand to act.
I should like to make a suggestion to the government. If and when the time comes that the need for conscription is indicated, if we are to maintain the balanced effort that has been achieved so successfully up to the present time regard must be given to the producers of foodstuffs. The production of foodstuffs is one of the most essential requirements of this wax. These men should be afforded all possible advantages; they should be given every facility and provided with every stimulus necessary to enable them to produce the surplus which is needed for the successful prosecution of this war. I think this government should see to it that there is no disproportion between the prices that the farmer receives for his products and what he must pay for his domestic wants and implements of production.
When the government is considering the conscripting of man-power it should be careful not to bring about a condition which will have an unbalancing effect upon our war effort. I should like to cite one case. I have a number of fishermen and farmers in my constituency who operate on a small scale. The man I have in mind was most provident. He had one son and he operated a small fishing industry. But he is now past his age of labour and his son is in the army. He has a boat and the necessary equipment to do a small amount of fishing, and now that the fishing season is coming on he has tried to have his son released from the army, but he has not been successful. This is only one of a number of cases in my constituency. This man cannot operate without the assistance of his son, and his operations are not large enough to warrant his hir-
The Address-Mr. McGarry

ing another man. Here is a man who should be a producer, but if his son is not released from the army he will probably be on relief. When this matter of conscription comes up for consideration I ask the government to see that the producers' man-power is not reduced to such a degree that they will not be able to produce the required surplus as well as their own domestic needs.

I could not tell you that. [ was interested in hearing what the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Macdonald) had to say the other day about the necessity of the government being vigilant in preparing facilities for ship repairs. In the light of What is happening off the Pacific coast it looks as though the day may come when the facilities he has in mind will be in great demand. In the historic town of Louisburg in my constituency there is a wonderful site for a dry dock. Nature herself laid out the site and has done most of the construction. Experts in the Department of Naval Services and the Department of Transport have visited that site, admired it, and reported back to the government. I do not know what has happened since, but in view of what is happening in the Pacific I would urge the government to look carefully into the possibility of constructing a ship repair plant at that site because there are strong indications that such a plant may be required on the Atlantic coast.
Allow me, Mr. Speaker, to say just one word more with regard to Canada's achievements in this war. I do not think this has been mentioned by any other speaker, and I shall take only a few minutes.
At the beginning of the war the government did not lose sight of the fact that some planning should be done for the day when the war is over. Some people disagree with that view. They say that we Should not consider postwar problems when we are in the midst of the conflict. I do not agree with this opinion. I agree, of course, that it should1 be the thought and purpose of every Canadian to prosecute this war vigorously to the very best of our ability. Nevertheless I think it is our duty to give consideration to and do some planning for the day when our soldiers come back to their civilian employment and when the work of manufacturing implements of destruction ceases-the day also when prices of commodities, which in wartime are bound to reach a higher level, recede once more to the economic levels of peacetime. I think some planning should be done to meet these events. The wartime prices and trade board has prevented the

profiteering and hoarding which obtained in the last war when we witnessed the disgraceful spectacle of individuals and corporations waxing fat on the sacrifices of the men who stood in arms against the foe. The ceiling which the board and the government have imposed upon commodity prices is a guard against inflation, and I think it will protect us in a great measure at least from a depression such as followed after the last war, and which brought suffering and privation almost equal to the horrors of war itself.
While in a democracy we have the right to engage in controversy and argue whether a certain way is right or wrong, our united purpose should now be to consider first our national responsibilities and to protect our democratic rights which are being attacked by the enemy who would, if possible, take them away from us. This is no time for bickering or carping criticism. Constructive criticism is helpful to the government and we should welcome it. AVhile we may have our controversies and arguments as to the right or wrong way of doing things, we should never forget that this is no ordinary war between nation and nation but a conflict between ideologies. On the one side we have democracy, which gives us all the rights and privileges that make life worth living. On the other side we have the totalitarian tyrants who would take away from us those rights and privileges, and who seek to destroy everything that is spiritual in man. That is the crisis we are facing and we might as well face it, realizing that we are witnessing the greatest tragedy of carnage which this world has ever seen. The ghost of that carnage is almost at our very doorstep. This is a time for us to coordinate our national efforts. Let us preserve our unity and go forward with a united' purpose and the single determination to win. If we do that, and1 if every Canadian will do his duty, we shall overthrow these tyrants who have gone absolutely mad in their desire for world domination.
I shall vote for the plebiscite. My constituency will give an affirmative answer. I trust my leader. He will not abuse the power he asks for. The people of my constituency have faith in his leadership, in war or in peace.
