Long before this, Mr. Acting Speaker, you will have concluded that every subject that can properly be debated on this motion so ably introduced by yourself as the member for Hull (Mr. Fournier), has long since been exhausted by the eloquence and logic of the members who have preceded me. Notwithstanding that, I am going to venture a few

The Address-Mr. McNiven
remarks at this time, and in case I should omit to do so at a later stage I state now that I intend to support the motion as introduced by yourself and seconded by the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald). I intend to vote against both amendments now before the house, notwithstanding that both of them may have some merit, but because undoubtedly they are a want of confidence motion in this government. Since I am fully persuaded that this government during its term of office has handled efficiently and well every situation that has arisen, I could not under the circumstances support anything that savoured of a vote of want of confidence.
Every candidate for an election, upon the acceptance of a party nomination thereby accepts the party's policy and the declarations of its leader. The policy and the declarations of the Liberal party and the declarations of our leader were well known and widely publicized throughout this country. For that reason, sir, I intend to support the plebiscite and to use every endeavour within my power to bring about a practically unanimous vote in the constituency which I represent-and I mean every section of that constituency. I am supported in the view that such will be the fact, for among the various resolutions that I have recently received was one from the German-Canadian club of our city supporting an all-out Canada war effort. I am further persuaded in that connection because of the declaration of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and various other ministers, that the taking of this plebiscite would not mean a sidgle day or hour of delay in the furthering and development of Canada's war effort.
The Prime Minister and the members of the government are capable men, sincere, honest, straightforward and loyal to both king and country; and they are the ones who, from the responsibility of their positions, are best equipped to know what is needed, what is essential in promoting a balanced, continuous war effort-balanced and continuous to the very end, no matter how long that may be. I am further convinced that the Prime Minister will sponsor and enact any and every measure that is essential to bring about ultimate victory.
In a recent issue of the magazine Liberty there appeared a biographical sketch of the Prime Minister written by Mr. Grattan O'Leary. After reviewing the events of what must be described as a colourful life, the distinguished author comments that the Prime Minister is possessed of something, a trait, a
characteristic, subtle and impossible to put into words, but which has had a genuine appeal to hundreds of thousands of people in this country over a long period of years and which his critics have been totally unable to understand or appreciate.
With deference to the distinguished author may I suggest that that subtle something ir the Prime Minister's character, which the author found so elusive, was very aptly expressed by Lord Tennyson when he penned these lines:
And, because right is right, to follow right
Were wisdom in the scorn of consequence.
This couplet expresses a whole political philosophy; it is a chart for personal guidance; and the Prime Minister's adherence to and his courage in the expression of its truth has inspired confidence in him in the minds of the Canadian people and has brought confusion to his critics and those whose standards of political life do not reach the pinnacle which he has achieved.
The publication of the census returns a few weeks ago brought some startling results in so far as we who reside in Saskatchewan are concerned, because by an alleged reduction in population that province will lose four of its representation in this house. The representation is now twenty-one, and with the realignment in Saskatchewan the membership will be reduced to seventeen. Our population in 1931 was 922,000, and for those hon. members who live in eastern Canada, may I say that our constitution provides for a quinquennial census. Because of that provision a census of the prairie provinces was taken in 1936, and in 1936 our population had shown an increase-930,893. But by June, 1941, our population had been reduced to 887,747, or a loss of approximately 43,000. Conditions following 1936, notwithstanding the catastrophe of 1937, improved from year to year. They were better in 1938; they were better again in 1939; and they showed a substantial improvement in 1940. Where and why, then, the loss? What is the answer? There can be only one answer and that is, the exigencies of war. Enlistments from our province approximate 35,000 in all the armed forces. Geography, our own economy, and the necessity of making large shipments of war materials to Britain and the European front precluded the development of war industries in Saskatchewan. But, patriotic to the core, our people have come east where war work was to be had; and I can say, from conversations with eastern industrialists, that they are glad to have the prairie dweller in their factories because of his resourcefulness and initiative.
The Address-Mr. McNiven

I protest most vigorously at any reduction in the membership of this house from the province of Saskatchewan, particularly at this time, and owing to the causes which I have already indicated. Prior to 1930 Saskatchewan was the third province in the dominion, and for the following five or six years that province experienced every kind of agricultural disaster that was ever conceived by the mind of man. Saskatchewan, however, is emerging from the effects and consequences of that disaster. While it is true that in that period the accumulated savings of bygone years have been swept away, two things stand out like a neon light in a black-out, that the fertility of our soil is unimpaired, and that the courage and spirit of our people remain unbroken. Our people look forward with confidence, faith and hope to the day when Saskatchewan will again occupy the proud position she once occupied in the galaxy of Canadian provinces. Saskatchewan will play a prominent part in the settlement of post-war problems; our wide open spaces, our resources, offer ample scope and opportunity for the industry of many millions. I appeal to hon. members, with their genius, their initiative, to find some means of avoiding the infliction of this penalty to which I have referred, upon a patriotic people at this time. What has been done before can be done again. In 1915, on the petition of this parliament, the British parliament amended the British North America Act in these terms:
51A. Notwithstanding anything in this act a province shall always be entitled to a number of members in the House of Commons not less than the number of senators representing such province.
I am not familiar with all the reasons which occasioned that amendment, but I would point out that it was made in war time and it had the effect of stabilizing the membership of this house in so far as certain provinces are concerned. I will not develop the point further at this time except to urge that, if our constitution as it stands at present makes imperative an adjustment or realignment of the membership of this house, we immediately initiate proceedings to amend our constitution so that we can postpone this until after the war when conditions have again become settled, and that the membership of this house remain as it now is.
By that same amendment the senatorial representation of Canada was fixed. Canada was divided into four divisions, the maritimes, Quebec, Ontario and the west, each with a senatorial representation of twenty-four. I am not going to suggest that the senatorial representation of any area should be cut down, but I do' say that the prairie provinces and 
British Columbia now have a population of nearly 3,300,000, almost equal to that of Ontario, and three times as great as that of the maritime provinces. Notwithstanding this, there has been no demand from the west for increased senatorial representation; that is due to our characteristic modesty. But I can say, sir, that the demand will become vocal and more and more insistent should this reduction of membership be forced upon us at this time. I think all will agree that that august body would be invigorated by the infusion of a little prairie vim, a little more prairie vigour, versatility and resourcefulness.
I would repeat now a statement which I made in the presence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) at Regina; there are far too many people in Ottawa occupying repon-sible positions who think that nothing good can be done outside this city. While this statement has particular reference to the Minister of Finance, it is not a criticism of one for whom I have a very high regard, and who has steadily grown in the estimation of the people of this country. But, sir, a constant appeal is being made for the purchase of war savings certificates and stamps. The individual who purchases these certificates must send to Ottawa and submit to weeks of delay before his certificate comes along. Why should these certificates not be sold in our banks and post offices, under such limitations as you will, so that the purchaser may have immediate concrete evidence of his patriotic impulse? Shortly afterwards, I heard over the radio an announcement by the United States authorities that war savings certificates could1 be purchased from the banks, from the post offices, and even from the letter carriers as they go from door to door. I therefore suggest that a similar practice be adopted in this country to encourage the sale of war savings certificates.
When the price ceiling was introduced, licences were required, and over 300,000 licences were issued to wholesalers and' retailers. They were all issued from Ottawa. The regional directors sat idly in their offices, impotent, unable to give information to the merchants who 'besieged them for it. When the army called for women recruits, it was announced in the press that applications would be received at military district headquarters. Later that was cancelled, and then it was to be at national registration headquarters. That was cancelled, and every woman in this country who desired to enlist in the army was required to send her application to Ottawa.
These are just a few examples of what I mean by centralization of everything in Ottawa.
I do not blame the ministers; they cannot know everything that goes on. But these are

The Address-Mr. McNiven
examples of the conduct, the intention and the desire of bureaucrats in responsible positions to extend their authority and expand their position, irrespective of the inconvenience caused to the general public. Washington is rapidly becoming the nerve centre of the war, and almost every day we 'hear announced in the press that non-war departments and those having to do with civilian life are being moved to New York, Philadelphia, Chicago and other centres in the United States. May I suggest to the government that a similar practice be followed here, that civilian departments be moved out from Ottawa to centres in other parts of Canada. This would obviate the necessity for continued temporary office construction in the capital and at the same time greatly relieve the Ottawa housing situation.
I mentioned a moment ago that certain facts, our geography, our economy and the necessities of war, had precluded our participation in the war industries up to the present time. However, the outbreak of war in the Pacific and the presence of U-boats on the Atlantic, in American waters, have substantially changed this picture. The Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) is efficiently energetic and is surrounded by capable men who doubtless have a full appreciation of this problem. They will have realized that of all Canada, the prairies are least vulnerable; and that of the prairies, Saskatchewan is in a favoured positiop in this regard. Our anxiety over the Pacific coast extends to the industries that have been established there, and immediately suggests that any additions or extensions or new industries should be established where they will be safe from possible attack; and that place, I submit, is on the prairies. In adopting such a policy we would be following what has been done in the United States, where already they have established many of their key industries in the middle west, in that part of their territory which corresponds to the province of Saskatchewan. The westward flow of materials made neeesssary by the outbreak of war in the Pacific again suggests the necessity and advisability of establishing industries on the prairies.
I make this suggestion, not from a monetary point of view, but from the innate desire of our people to have a larger place in the war picture and to use their experience, energy, inclination and training in order that they may be of assistance at this time. Just here I want to thank the Minister of Munitions and Supply for establishing Regina Industries for the manufacture of gun carriages for antitank guns. That plant is not yet in production, but I fully understand why that is so.
They advertised for labour and received over five hundred applications from men on the prairies who had machine-shop experience. Many of them, it is true, were rusty, but they soon acquired skill and speed. Industry in the east has drawn heavily upon our population, but I submit that as a principle it is still preferable to move industry to labour rather than to take labour to industry.
The big industrialist who has been favoured with large war contracts has not farmed out the manufacture of component parts as he was expected and instructed to do. As a result, there is still a wealth of equipment and skill in the prairie regions which have not been used. A similar condition obtains in the United States, and only recently I heard over the radio that the small munition plants and small machine-shops were making a united, vigorous protest to the United States congress, urging that the policy of centralizing industry had brought them to the point of bankruptcy and was militating against the American war effort. Industrial development in Canada has reached astronomical proportions, running into billions of dollars. Notwithstanding that, I fear hon. members will doubt my word when I say that the only contracts awarded in the province of Saskatchewan have been as follow's: John East, of Saskatoon, $65,000, being a sub-contract from Manitoba Bridge; Richardson Road Machinery, $150,000 for trailers; Northwest Iron Works, $70,000 for steel rollers; Northwest Iron Works, $4,800, being a sub-contract from the Ogden Shops, Calgary; and G. and G. of Prince Albert, who have had a few small contracts from Canada Car and Foundry at Fort William. I do not include in this list Regina Industries, but I do say that full use is not being made of the inclination, the training, the ability and the resources of our province.
About two weeks ago parliament played host tc- a representative group of Saskatchewan citizens who made a submission to the government with regard to agriculture. It was one of the largest delegations to visit Ottawa in recent years. The presentation was carefully prepared, logically arranged, and cogently presented. It was an unfolding of the democratic system; and in this time of stress and strain it is good to know that there are still countries where the people can approach their government without personal danger. The representations of this delegation were courteously received by the government, and from conversations I had with delegates I would judge that they departed for their homes with a new conception of the many problems confronting a government in a rapidly changing

The Address-Mr. McNiven

world. This is characteristic of that sweet sense of reasonableness which always actuates the western mind.
Prairie dwellers know that western wheat is the best food product in the world. They know, too, that the time will oome when that food product will be needed by our allies, as it will be needed in the postwar period. We know the important part played by wheat in the last war. Sir George Paish, the eminent British economist, told a number of us here in 1938 that if it had not been for the productivity of the western plains and the ability of the British navy to transport our wheat to England, that country would have been starved into submission in 1916 and again in 1917. Wheat was the only commodity that was commandeered in the last war. The United States farmer received from $1 to $1.50 a bushel more for his wheat than the western agriculturist received, but the prairie farmer smilingly accepted that reduction in price as his opportunity to render national service. Wheat is temporarily a drug on the market, and that being so, the farmer does not ask for that parity of price which is enjoyed by Canadian labour and industry. He asks merely for a price that will enable him to continue as a productive unit until such time as his commodity is again in universal demand. Such a plea, presented on national grounds and from patriotic motives, must not remain) unanswered, and I am sure the Canadian people generally will approve the granting of the request presented by this delegation.
Ouirs is a peculiar situation. We are still subject to recurring periods of drought over wide areas. Every farmer, every farm, is a national asset. He produces what is required to maintain the body and fertilize the mind, and for that reason must be maintained as a national resource.
For this reason, sir, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has become the magna oharta of western agriculture, serving and fulfilling a long-felt want. The loss of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act would create consternation and dismay on the prairie farm. Of all the innovations and policies developed by the dynamic Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to stabilize agriculture, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act still holds the spotlight as accomplishing the greatest good for the greatest number.

The government is to be commended for the construction of the chain of airports between Edmonton and Alaska. The purpose is obvious, and that purpose was confirmed by what happened on December 7. Supplies will be needed in the far north, and the integrated purpose of the Canadian and United States governments make imperative the immediate construction of a highway connecting the centres of production in the middle western states with Canada's and America's vulnerable hinterland. That construction is a mammoth undertaking and, in the light of existing events, has become an imperative necessity.
May I suggest to the government that, in the choice of a route, scenic and tourist possibilities be overlooked. This is no tourist expedition, and the ambitions and animosities of local areas should not be considered. The route to be constructed should be the one which is capable of quick, easy, speedy construction, and will demand the smallest part of the taxpayers' dollar. As fulfilling all those specifications, I suggest to the government the prairie route as being best calculated to serve the demand.
As residents of the prairies, we share the anxieties of the people in British Columbia with regard to their Japanese problem. The revelations respecting Pearl Harbour have justified that anxiety, an anxiety which I may say to you, sir, is most real, and not imaginary.
I would urge-the government that it ought not to hesitate to remove the Japanese from points of danger in British Columbia, and, if necessary, a safe place can and will be found for them on the prairies. Consequences of delay are hard to visualize. I can best repeat the words used on one occasion by Mr. Churchill-"There is not a week, nor a day nor an hour to be lost."
A cloud no bigger than a man's hand has recently appeared on the political horizon, a cloud reminiscent of the most sinister political alliance that ever darkened the pages of Canadian history. The hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) scented its presence the other afternoon, and with his keen analytical	mind depicted some of its
possibilities. In 1911, in Quebec the Nationalist cry was anti-imperialism, and in Ontario the Tory slogan was, "No truck or trade with the Yankees." Following 1911, these antagonistic doctrines found common ground. Messrs. Bourassa and LaVergne refused appointment in Sir Robert Borden's cabinet. They were allowed to select and they chose Pelletier, Nantel and Blondin, all Nationalists, and later, in 1916, Mr. Albert Sevigny, an outstanding Nationalist, was named Speaker of the house.

The Address-Mr. McNiven
In September, 1914, after the outbreak of the last war, Mr. Bourassa said in his paper, Le Devoir, that it was-
1-Canada's national duty to contribute according to her resources, and by fitting means of action to the triumph and especially to the endurance of the combined efforts of France and England. I have not written and will not write one line, one word to condemn the sending of Canadian troops to Europe.
Estimable, indeed! His conversion, however, was Short-lived, for from 1915 on, both in the press and on the platform we find him in unmeasured terms condemning Canada's participation in any of Britain's wars. His shafts of criticism were levelled at Sir Wilfrid, and reached their climax in September, 1916, when he declared:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier is the most nefarious man in the province of Quebec, yes, in the whole of Canada.
On Wednesday last this same Mr. Bourassa emerged from retirement, rose from a sickbed, and with something of his old time vigour, combined in a single address both the arguments which in 1911 were used to undermine Sir Wilfrid in Ontario, and again in Quebec. What did Bourassa say on this occasion? As reported in a boxed position on the centre of the front page of the Montreal Gazette, he said:
Canada will be annexed by the United States within ten years.
The present policy of the Canadian government is not dictated by London, but by Washington.
Borden and Meighen were both more honest than the present government leaders.

speechtext:
"Hear, hear", someone says. He is just a little too early; I shall deal with that later.
Living in the past, this crafty old campaigner made a double-barrelled appeal to the anti-imperialists of Quebec, and to the British whose roots are deep m British traditions, by sowing seeds of distrust of our American neighbour. He likewise endeavoured to undermine the confidence of the Canadian people in the honesty of members of the administration, and his thought in that direction was similar to the invective he employed against Sir Wilfrid in 1916.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, why was such prominence given to these thoughts in the Montreal Gazette? Did that newspaper have an objective similar to that which brought Bourassa out into the limelight once again? In its editorial page, on the following day, it is true that they acclaimed those portions in which he tendered sage advice to some of his compatriots. But it is equally true that
44561-39J
they registered only mild disagreement with the more insidious part of the address.
Commenting on the same speech, the Globe and Mail said editorially:
What will cause special anguish at Ottawa was the declaration of his belief that Sir Robert Borden and Arthur Meighen were more honest in their attitudes than our present ministers.
I wonder what standard Bourassa had in mind when he used that language? I wonder what was passing through the mind of the editor of the Globe and Mail when he quoted it with such gleeful approval? I ask you, Mr. Speaker, was it the War-time Elections Act of 1917? On the other hand, was it the famous Hamilton speech, or was it the speech delivered by the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen in the Quebec by-election in 1926? Perchance was it the famous "last gasp" speech delivered by the right bon. gentleman on January 27, 1942? Or possibly it was that amazing contradiction of past performances and past utterances delivered by the right hon. gentleman on February 3, 1942. Mr. Speaker, I leave the answer and the comparison of standards to you and to other members of this house. Again I ask you: What is the purpose and objective of this mentality which has in the past created so much trouble for this government and indirectly hindered the war effort?
I shall call another witness who has been motivated by similar ideas. Premier Hep-bum must have known or should have known that his declarations against the United States navy would cause anxiety and distrust in the minds of Canadians with regard to our great ally and would create antagonisms on the other side of the line. The Winnipeg Free Press, commenting upon his action in that connection, made the following statement:
The harm done by Mr. Hepburn will outlive and outlast any amends offered by Canada.
On page 2 of the Montreal Gazette of this morning I find the following in "Lights and Shadows" by L. S. B. Shapiro:
Mr. Hepburn's feat: It would be nice if Mr. Hepburn's bright little escapade of last week could be laughed off and dismissed merely as part of the price we have to pay for having an aggressive prankster in a responsible position. In trying to be as lively as possible on all occasions, Sir. Hepburn has provided the dominion with a few guffaws and not a few headaches, the most violent of which is his current criticism of the United States navy.
I fear, however, that this one is not to be laughed off so easily. A lot of people I know in Rew York and Washington are laughing very bitterly and they show no sign of stopping.
And again:
More important than these examples of ruffled feeling is the comment of Fletcher Pratt, the
The Address-Mr. McNiven

noted American military expert. Mr. Pratt observes the U.S. navy has not attacked the main Japanese fleet for precisely the same reason that the Canadian army in Britain has not attacked the Germans who are only fifty miles distant from some of the Canadian encampments.
Thus we begin to find ourselves in a battle of recrimination over our beautiful, undefended border while we are still losing the war to the axis. A Hitler agent couldn't have done as well in a year of trying.
I mentioned a moment ago that a cloud no bigger than a man's hand had appeared on the political horizon. Knowing that the friendly relations between Canada and the United States is primarily the accomplishment of the Prime Minister, as was abundantly attested to last evening by the President of the United States, I ask you, Mr. Speaker: Are the critics of the Prime Minister developing a new line of attack regardless of its effect upon our war effort and our friendly relations with our greatest ally, the United States? I cannot believe that the retention of the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen as leader, the reappearance of Bourassa in the limelight and Hepburn's recent outbursts are mere coincidence. Rather would I believe that the opponents of this government, having failed to stampede the people on the plebiscite and conscription issues, are now trying the old game of 1911 by bringing about the unity of the Nationalist group in Quebec and the narrow-minded persons who always look askance at the United States because of the fact that a close association with that country might infringe upon the monopolies which they enjoy. Truly it is a strange alliance- the imperialistic Mr. Meighen-the anti-war Mr. Bourassa!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say at the very outset of my speech that if Canada is not one hundred per cent in the war to-day, it is the duty of this parliament to remove impediments and close the gaps immediately, for in the words of Prime Minister Churchill there is not a week nor a day nor an hour to be lost. If we hesitate, if we delay, if we try to conserve our resources, and if likewise our allies should employ less than their maximum in this struggle, who is to say that we shall not be driven out of the Orient, out of Africa, yea, even out of Europe? Contemplating now such a situation, is it not imperative for our survival that we throw the entire strength of the nation immediately into this struggle? In war there is no second heat, no return game, no second chance.
The hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght), speaking in this debate on February 12, referred to the speech from the throne in 1936 in which was forecast a bill to create parliamentary secretaryships. I have pressed for this enlarged representation and participation by members on so many occasions in this parliament and elsewhere that I do not propose at this time to repeat what I have said. But the reference calls to mind the statement that I made in the auditorium of the city hall in Guelph when I was a candidate in the 1925 election. I was advocating the return of the Liberal government on a platform of which one plank was senate reform. During the course of preparing my speech to-day I was

The Address-Mr. Gladstone
seeking for confirmation of that plank, and I found it in Hansard of January 12, 1926, at page 105, in a speech delivered by Mr. C. W. Bell, then member for Hamilton West. Mr. Bell referred to a speech that had been made by the then Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in a hockey arena in London, Ontario, on October 16, 1925, during the election campaign. The words of the Prime Minister, as quoted by Mr. Bell, were as follows:
Only a few days ago a number of senators were appointed. Every one has given me his pledged word he will be prepared, once a measure passes the Commons, to give it his support. Subsequent senators will be appointed with that understanding, and as Providence takes away a few of the older members, you will have a Senate pledged to bring about the reforms for which the administration stands.
I have the utmost confidence that this is a matter which will be receiving the attention of the Prime Minister in due time.
I sometimes wonder whether it is an evidence of strength or of weakness in our cabinet make-up that we do not have family rows and resignations. Shake-ups are common in the British cabinet. I sometimes wonder whether we are not too hesitant about creating occasions for by-elections. Who will say that the recent by-elections were not without profit right across Canada in bringing all the diversified factors of our war effort into the open for discussion and decision? Boldness of policy in this respect should strengthen any government. Our democracy will be more secure as we trust the people more. Therefore I would suggest to the Prime Minister, as a humble supporter of his, that the undoubted confidence in which he is presently held by the electors will be heightened if he will more often furnish occasions on which the electors can pass judgment on the record of his government.
There is opportunity now for the rejuvenation of the cabinet, with so many senate vacancies inviting it. Whose move is it? Don't too many speak at once-make it easy for the Prime Minister. Seriously, however, these days call for forceful and resourceful men, the type that, unflinching before Hitler and his gang, would spring at them and smash them a black-out.
The two great instruments for moulding public opinion and maintaining and uplifting the morale of the nation in this time of stress and during occasional dark days of near panic are the press and the radio. Canada has been blessed over the years in having finely conducted newspapers. Readers have been able to place reliance on the news reports of events, local, national and world-wide. But one wonders sometimes whether the merging of ownerships for exclusiveness of newspaper field has
not given rise to some catering to interests and the use of the newspaper columns to promote interests and to promote the views of powerful and influential groups.
More explicitly what I have in mind is the colouring of news, over-emphasizing certain features and suppressing or merging other features, depending upon some possible objective to be attained. Perhaps I should give some instances of what I have in mind.
Take (1) the speech by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Fraser). One paper refers to his speech as a burlesque, accompanied by prolonged applause and deskthumping. As a matter of fact, the deskthumping coincided with a statement which was not mentioned at all in the editorial, namely, that some persons would conscript youth to fight for their dollars.
(2)	A most capable member, of undoubted sincerity, in his speech dealt with a tendency of some papers to belittle members of parliament. His was a considered and reasoned argument. One paper has an isolated comment, quoting only the following of his words: "We may be a mediocre lot. God help us, I know we are."
(3)	Two morning newspapers reporting the speeches in parliament of the preceding day, used the following front page headlines respectively: (a) "More Liberals from Quebec tell Commons they oppose conscription for overseas"; (b) "Five Quebec members back plebiscite plan-three others express opposition in Commons debate."
It is to be regretted if there is any trend towards colouring the news in Canada, even in isolated places; and should the colouring of news be employed to the extent of possibly undermining the nation during war time, it ought to become a matter for government attention, looking, for instance, to an amendment to the libel section of the criminal code. Not being a lawyer, I would not assume any competence to pass on legal questions, but as a layman I simply suggest that persistent colouring of news in a way that is detrimental to the morale of the nation in time of war ought not to be permitted regardless of the long-accepted principle of the freedom of the press. Defamatory libel is defined in section 317 of the criminal code in these words:
A defamatory libel is matter published, without legal justification or excuse, likely to injure the reputation of any person by exposing him to hatred, contempt or ridicule, or designed to insult the person of or concerning whom it is published.
Provided that the scope of this definition could be and were enlarged to include the national safety, then the colouring of the reports of the proceedings of parliament would
The Address-Mr. Gladstone

be an offence under section 322 of the criminal code which reads:
No one commits an offence by publishing in good faith, for the information of the public, a fair report of the proceedings of the Senate or House of Commons, or any committee thereof, or of any council or assembly aforesaid, or any committee thereof, or of the public proceedings, preliminary or final, heard before any court exercising judicial authority, nor by publishing, in good faith, any fair comment upon any such proceedings.
I would wish this allusion to the press to be regarded as of a more or less hypothetical nature and most certainly as in no way critical of those men and women who are in the press gallery of parliament, but nevertheless as a warning to their editors that theirs is the high mission of maintaining and upbuilding the morale of the nation during the war years.
Mr. Speaker, the true implication of certain portions of the speech of the hon. member for Northumberland, as reported at page 331 of Hansard were not grasped, or were ignored in some press reports. I wish to quote one paragraph of this speech; but before doing so, let me explain, for any one who may not know, the meaning or significance of two of the terms he used. "Who's Who" contains a list of directors, industrialists and financiers in Canada, showing the company or companies with which each is associated; and where he used the word "empire" he referred to investments or dollars, if you will. He said:
Let me go further and say to them, that if I owned an empire such as "Who's Who" says they own, I would want to conscript everybody in Canada to defend it. And, Mr. Speaker, if 1 had their mentality not only would I wish to conscript-insist upon conscripting-every man in Canada to defend that empire, but I would go farther and spend every dollar I could to create in this country in the minds of the people a situation which would delude and deceive them into conscripting people to defend my empire.
My purpose in referring to the speech of the hon. member for Northumberland is to lay the groundwork for my wholehearted support of any sound proposal for higher pay for the men who go forth to risk their lives for us all. Such a proposal was so splendidly set out in a speech by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver), as reported in Hansard at page 387, that I cannot do better than quote what he said:
Right here I should like to make a suggestion in regard to the armed forces. Many of those who have stayed at home have earned good wages. Some have spent them; others-many- have accumulated savings. I would urge, Mr. Speaker, that a savings fund should be set up for the armed forces. I would urge that every member of our armed forces while serving in Canada, should receive an additional $1 per day, and, while in active service overseas, an addi-

tional $2 per day. These savings should not be paid now, but at the end of the war. When the boys return, some will want to complete their education. Many of them will marry. Certainly all of them will find it difficult to get back into civilian life. None of the money would have to be paid now. This would not detract from the war effort. It would be no hardship to continue war-time taxation for a few years after the war. There is another feature about this. The proposed payments would establish a tremendous reservoir of consumer demand for goods at a time when this country will badly need a consumer demand for goods to start its industries going again in peace-time operations, turning over from wartime operations.
We have a study underway. It will be a progressive study of means of assisting men, both of the armed forces and of those who have been diverted to war activities, back to a normal civilian life. Here is the place to apply the suggestion of the hon. member for Parry Sound as to the creation of parliamentary secretaryships. The study is being made under the direction of the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), in whose ability we have the utmost confidence, and he is supported by an able committee of civil servant experts. There might, however, be some worth-while advantage in bringing to the assistance of this committee a few of the elected representatives of the people, men who at the next election will have to go back and account to the people for what they have done in the direction of providing for a speedy and decent rehabilitation of our returned men.
To turn next to agriculture, the condition of our great industry of agriculture is one which demands tackling by methods which so far have not been employed. Speaking of Ontario agriculture, I would say that prices being realized to-day are at a fairly reason. able level having regard to what the working man supporting a family can afford to pay. But where is the margin to the farmer to erect a new bam or even to reroof the old barn, or to replace worn-out implements, or to instal modern equipment, or to do the many things that would be profitable to our industries in supplying needed materials? Men are leaving the farms for the one and only reason that it is not possible for them to maintain those farms as their fathers and their grandfathers were able to maintain them, progressively, making farming in reality a way of life. I submit, therefore, that in relation to agriculture we must face the perplexing situation where the working man can hardly afford to pay more and the farmer cannot make ends meet at present prices for the food products of Ontario mixed farming.
Seemingly the experts in economics have not yet arrived at a solution of this problem,

The Address-Mr. Gladstone
unless perhaps they are unwilling to do so. Here, again, I see an opportunity for the application of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Pariy Sound as to the creation of parliamentary secretaryships looking to representation in the administration for eastern agriculture. We have a most capable Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), but I think he will admit that the problem of the western wheat surplus, coupled with the destitution of western farmers in drought areas, has made very heavy demands upon his time. I am not informed as to what use is being made of the Ontario Agricultural College at Guelph, the most outstanding college of its kind in the world, towards meeting the economic situation of the eastern agriculturists; but I will say that if the services of the president and staff, who are all trained in agricultural economics, are not being used to the fullest extent possible, they should be.
For the sake of the farmer, some means must be found to make his dollar go further. For the sake of the working man in our factory, the farmer must be put in a position to buy more freely the implements, the equipment and the materials the making of which gives employment in our towns and cities. We ought never to forget the old saying that whenever the farmer prospers, everyone prospers.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson), speaking in this debate on January 26, as reported at page 25 of Hansard used these words:
When the Union army of volunteers was in desperate condition, President Lincoln is reported to have said:	.
Voluntarism is the unprincipled dodge of cowardly politicians. It has ground up the choicest seed of the nation. It has consumed the young, the generous, the patriotic, the intelligent, and the brave, and it has wasted the best moral, social, and political elements of the republic, and left the cowards, the shirkers, and the money makers to stay at home and procreate their kind.
A rather extensive search has been made in the library of parliament at Ottawa, in the library of congress at Washington and by noted authorities on Lincoln such as Mr. Grant Dexter of the Winnipeg Free Press and Mr. Dave Elman of the Hobby Lobby programme, Radio City, New York, but without success so far in confirming that these words were used in a speech by Lincoln. Be that as it may, however, I am sure that many of my electors of Wellington South would feel that there is more truth than fiction in these words as applicable to the present war.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), speaking here on February 10, gave a most comprehensive review of Canada's contribution to date in all our fields of service. It is to be hoped that his speech has been read by very many Canadians. It reveals a marvellous undertaking and accomplishment to date by Canada, and1 gives proof of greater momentum for growing achievement in the future in all spheres of our planned service. Every hon. member has, I am sure, been impressed by the sincerity, strength and determination of our Minister of National Defence. Following a most thorough review of the results of voluntary enlistment, and after urging support of the plebiscite to give the government a free hand for whatever changes may become necessary, the minister said, as reported at page 455 of Hansard:
I prefer the voluntary method if it works, and I shall do all I can to make it work. At the same time, we cannot know what is ahead and I feel impelled to say-here I can speak only for myself-that if the voluntary system does not meet the needs of the fateful days before us, then I shall feel it my duty as part of my responsibility to advocate the adoption of the other method.
For myself, I wish to subscribe to the view stated and the position taken by the Minister of National Defence. I hold a decided preference for the system of draft followed1 in the United States, where some of more mature years are called to the service before exhausting entirely the cream of the youth. We are suffering to-day from discouraging methods of recruiting followed during the earlier days of the war. Many fine young men were turned back for reasons which appeared unjustifiable, and having gone to some other war service or to preparation where still higher skill is involved, they are loath to offer themselves again immediately. Some badge of recognitioh is certainly due to them to lift from them the stigma attaching to slackers. Many such are waiting to be told where they can best serve. Pushing men around is something more easily said than done on a national scale. Something more definite and intensive is required in the way of system in directing them where their duty lies, whether on the farm, in the factory or in some branch of the armed services.
I come now to a phase of the discussion which carries a risk of misunderstanding, but inasmuch as some of my electors have not the opportunity I have of knowing the situation, I feel that I owe it to them to be frank for the good of all Canada. Preliminary to a discussion of our Canadian partnership let
The Address-Mr. Gladstone

me repeat in effect the words of a great Canadian of the present day of French ancestry: "Your attitude towards the war outside of Canada is motivated partly by sentiment whereas our attitude comes more through judgment." While no doubt he is largely correct, I would say that there are strong evidences of a good deal of sentiment for the old land in the French-speaking parts of Canada since the king and1 queen visited Quebec and the queen spoke to the cheering crowds in French. Yes, I stand for a one hundred per cent participation by Canada in this world struggle. We must trust our government and our high military officials as to methods and progressive development, for they alone can know the secret plans of allied strategy. Decisions cannot be based alone on the view of the member for Wellington South, or the views of the electors of Wellington county, or of the province of Ontario, or of the province of Quebec, or of any other province. Total war requires total harmonization of objective and effort within Canada, plus careful coordination with the plans of the supreme command of the allies. Total war cannot be achieved amidst discord, passive resistance or indifference. War to be efficient can give no place for appeasement, because appeasement lulls, quiets and reduces striking force. I am certain that the electors I have the honour to represent have no use for any policy or attitude of appeasement. I am equally certain that they will approve all reasonable means to bring every province and all persons of whatever race into cooperation for the fullest possible use of Canada's entire resources of wealth, materials, man-power and woman-power. Firm believers in democracy and democractic government are fond of saying, "Trust the people." But in war time when so much relating to military preparations and operations must be kept secret, it is equally true that the people must .more than at other times trust the government. For this very reason of secrecy many facts concerning the war programme cannot be made known, even to private members of parliament. We as members have trusted the Prime Minister and his cabinet, and in turn we are grateful that our constituents have trusted us.
I have spoken of the need for cooperation. There cannot and must not be any varying degrees of cooperation by the provinces. Canada must be a unit in this struggle to preserve freedom, liberty and justice as these have been vouchsafed wherever the British flag has flown. This war must be won. Canada must do her full part, and we hope and pray that she will do so with the fullest cooperation of all her people.

The plebiscite is designed surely to achieve that united effort. Count not the expense if Canadians everywhere, English-speaking and French-speaking alike, will by their votes remove any hindrance to total war. And total war demands total participation of all Canadians, whether in Guelph, Toronto, Montreal, Quebec, Halifax, Vancouver or elsewhere. There are, I fear, those in Ontario who misjudge Quebec because they do not understand Quebec. They have not the opportunity that members of parliament have of mingling in a social way and in conference on affairs of state with many of the altogether likable, fine and most capable members from that province, whose mother tongue is French but who for the most part speak English almost as fluently as we of Anglo-Saxon ancestry. It would seem appropriate here to quote from the British North America Act. section 133:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of the parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec. . . .
The memories of the War-time Elections Act of 1917, and of the methods employed by the Union government in 1917 and 1918 to enforce the Military Service Act still rankle the French-Canadians. Knowing of the unhealed wounds from those days the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe felt compelled to define and limit Quebec's participation when war was declared on Germany in 1939. As recorded on September 9 at page 68 of Hansard of the second session of that year, he said:
The whole province of Quebec-and I speak with all the responsibility and all the solemnity I can give to my words-will never agree to accept compulsory service or conscription outside Canada. I will go farther than that: when X say the whole province of Quebec, I mean that I personally agree with them. I am authorized by my colleagues in the cabinet from the province of Quebec-the veteran leader of the Senate, my good friend and colleague, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), my friend and fellow townsman and colleague, the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power)-to say that we will never agree to conscription and will never be members or supporters of a government that will try to enforce it. Is that clear enough?
A few months later, in March, 1940, a general election was held. I have before me now two important pieces of advertising used in the constituency of Wellington South during that campaign. One was issued in my behalf, as Liberal candidate, while the other was issued in behalf of my opponent, the National Government candidate. Each carries in bold type the words "Without conscription." It is a truism, I believe, that the giving of this pledge by the two national leaders was due entirely to the fact that

The Address-Mr. Gladstone
Canada is a partnership of the two great races. More accurately, perhaps, the pledge was due directly to the ill-feeling engendered by the roughshod methods employed to enforce conscription in Quebec during the last great war. I realize that many electors in Wellington South are of the opinion that the government should not be bound by its "no conscription" pledge at a time when the very existence of freedom is at stake. Other electors hold strongly to the opposite opinion. The cabinet is unanimous that nothing should limit Canada's part in the war, and accordingly they are asking the electors, by means of a plebiscite, to cancel the election pledge of "no conscription" and thereby give them a free hand in whatever direction may become necessary in future to maintain a total war effort. After all, does not total war for Canada resolve itself down to a means of enlisting, not compelling, the cooperation of the two great races of this nation?
I have spoken of the lasting resentment in Quebec against the methods employed to enforce conscription in the last war. I have quoted from the speech of the late Minister of Justice, made at the outbreak of the present war, in which he declared most emphatically, "We will never agree to conscription." Today we who are in intimate contact with hon. members from Quebec are heartened by evidence of a changed attitude in Quebec. We have growing confidence that if we employ methods acceptable to her people, Quebec will stand shoulder to shoulder with Englishspeaking Canada for whatever service and wherever Canadians are called in this grim struggle. This changed attitude is reflected in the speech recently made in the house by a French-speaking member, the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Yeniot), who, as reported at page 512 of Hansard said:
We do recognize that the best way to defeat our enemy is to fight him outside of Canada and to prevent him from reaching our shores. To this end we are prepared to give freely of our lives and to the limit of our man-power and of our meagre means. But we want no more guns and no more bayonets hacking down our youth like wild beasts in our hills and our forests. We have open minds, but the way to convince us is not by making us guzzle it, by ramming conscription down our throats.
I cannot leave this section of my speech, Mr. Speaker, without paying the highest possible tribute to the memory of a great Canadian who is with us no more, the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe. The quotation I have read from his speech on the declaration of war ought, in all fairness, not to be read apart from the whole argument of that speech. Knowing the people of his province better than any other person in or out of 44561-40
parliament; knowing the discord that had been aroused by the endeavour to force conscription upon Quebec in 1917 and 1918, he stood adamant against a revival of such circumstances. His very soul spoke in a plea for methods in this war that would line up his compatriots with English-speaking Canada unitedly in this struggle. So I wish to leave with you some other words of this great Canadian, as they appear at page 69 of Hansard for 1939, second session:
God give Canadians the light which will indicate to them where their duty lies in this hour of trial so that our children and our children's children may inherit a land where freedom and peace shall prevail, where our social, political and religious institutions may be secure and from which the tyrannical doctrines of nazism and communism are forever banished. Yes, God bless Canada. God bless our queen. God bless our king.
I notice that my allotted time in this debate has almost elapsed, but if the house will bear with me for a few minutes I shall mention, without much elaboration, some other relevant factors in this debate on total war.
The word " communism " appears in a quotation I used a few moments ago. That reference, no doubt, has to do with the insidious propaganda that was waged over the world a few years back. All that can be and is forgotten to-day in our acclaim for the marvellous defence of Russian soil against the German war machine. That defence surely demonstrates to the world that Russia was not lying dormant. It is irrefutable evidence of what was taking place within her own borders, scientifically, industrially and in a disciplinary way.
In wars of other days a $20 suit, a $30 gun and a little "forming fours" made a man a soldier. To-day it is entirely different. War to-day requires a man of high intelligence to operate a Bren gun or a 50-ton tank, or to pilot a $100,000 bomber. I ask the armchair critics to contemplate just what modern warfare means in ships, guns, tanks, explosives, bombers, fighters; in training, and in all the organization and facilities for production. I ask them to inform themselves reliably of what Canada has done to date and what we are committed to do in the programme mapped out now for the period ending March, 1943, as to both men and materials. I ask them to remember that all our reverses to date in this war have been due to a shortage of munitions, not to a shortage of man-power. I ask them not to overlook the fact that Canada has been supplying munitions in huge quantities to the British isles, Russia, Africa, and the far east, even to the extent of leaving ourselves short. I ask them to note that there has been an upsurge in recruiting during recent

The Address-Mr. Gladstone

weeks, in excess of our facilities to train men. The winter-fair building at Guelph has had to be reopened during recent weeks as a training centre to accommodate the overflow from the Chatham and Kitchener camps.
This week every person who has means will enter the war in the victory loan campaign. At Guelph the whole strength of my riding is being organized under the able leadership of an outstanding citizen, Mr. W. P. Gamble, and they will by hard work go over the top. Here I would give the highest praise to the Globe and Mail for the tremendous boost it has given the campaign to-day in the striking display occupying the entire front page of its paper. The press is powerful, so powerful that, if so inclined, it can in a week lift the morale of the people one hundred per cent. That would go a long way toward maintaining a one hundred per cent war effort in Canada. Our hearts are saddened when we know that many fine young Canadians already have made the supreme sacrifice. Their places must and will be filled over there, and additional units to Canada's maximum will be sent. We must and will have reinforcements for every emergency. May God guide us and keep us faithful through the dark days, as we struggle on toward victory and the preservation of our right to live as free people.
