speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is almost four weeks since this debate began, and I hesitate to take the time of t'he house to speak, particularly when I realize that a great deal of important legislation is pending. I have, however, been asked from time to time why there is such delay in taking the vote on the plebiscite. Probably few people realize that it is first necessary to dispose of the motion we are now discussing before the government is in a position to introduce legislation making provision for the vote.
My observations with reference to the plebiscite itself will be very brief. When it was first mentioned there was a great deal of discussion and1 opposition, but I feel that as the weeks and days pass, that opposition diminishes, and11 am sure when the vote comes it will be accepted by a heavy affirmative vote. I know I shall do all in my power toward that end.
I do not believe conscription was mentioned during the last campaign in my constituency. I know I did not mention it, and I believe I can say the same for my opponent. Therefore conscription was not an issue, except as it was made one by the platforms of both parties. Each member is bound by the pledges made by his party, irrespective of whether he raises the question or not.

We are also told that the vote on the plebiscite will cost a large amount of money. It is true that the vote will cost about fifteen cents or twenty cents per person. Will any of those people who have been so provocative in their language respecting the cost of the plebiscite say that it is not worth twenty cents to them to know that a pledge given by a public man, not on a minor but on a major issue involving life itself, will not be broken without first appealing to the people to whom that pledge was given? Anyone who has studied the life of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) will agree with me that he has always been prepared to trust the people. I believe this is a question where we should not be guided in our decision by the request of othdrs; it is a question where our consciences should be our guide. If we permit our consciences to be our guide in respect of this question, I am sure none of us will look back and regret any action he has taken.
The following words from Shakespeare's "Hamlet" are a good guide to all of us in deciding questions of this kind:
This above all: to thine own self be true,
And it must follow, as the night the day,
Thou canst not then be false to any man.
The people I represent are satisfied with nothing less than a total effort. I believe there may be some difference of opinion as to how that objective is to be attained. A demand is raised in many parts, particularly in the urban area, that we should have a greater effort, including the conscription of man-power. If we listened to those who volunteer information, and those who tell us what they think we should do, we might consider that that is the predominant opinion. But when we make personal inquiries and investigate for ourselves we find quite often that that feeling is not so intense.
In fact, after making a survey of my constituency, I am doubtful if a vote on conscription, without including the conscription of wealth, would receive a favourable reply. If is interesting to study the response in the various parts of the province with respect to the advertisement carried in the Globe and Mail. This advertisement was carried in five local papers in my constituency of Simcoe North. My estimation is that in my constituency the advertisement in question went into approximately 6,000 homes. Hon. members will probably be surprised to learn that while those 6,000 homes were asked to write their federal member requesting him to do certain things, I received only thirty-four newspaper clippings. In addition, I received about twelve letters, but some of those were opposed to the advertisement, and others

The Address-Mr. McCuaig
agreed with it only if conscription of wealth were included.
I believe it is the duty of every hon. member as best he can to ascertain the wishes of his constituents. But he should also be guided by the information he receives from those charged with the responsibility of carrying on our war effort. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has made it clear that up to the present time we are obtaining by the voluntary system all the men we require. He has added that he prefers the voluntary system, if it works, and that he will do all he can to see that it does work. Although acknowledging the need for men, he emphasized the need for the production of food and weapons of war, as our contribution as one of the members of a team of united nations.
The message that General McNaughton gave to the soldiers at Christmas has already been put on Hansard. In that message he praised the Canadian soldier and stated that new units and formations and reserves would arrive as quickly as ships could be found to bring them. I should like to place upon Hansard an editorial which appeared in the Windsor Daily Star of February 10 as follows:
If anyone knows what is needed to win this war, it is Lieutenant-General A. G. L. McNaughton, general officer commanding the Canadian corps. The fact that one of his first acts after returning to Canada on furlough was to visit industrial plants turning out military equipment, coupled with his comments on this phase of our war effort, indicate the important place in his mind which armaments occupy. He has borne out what those closely in touch with the war situation have been saying all along. What our men need is equipment and more equipment. He does not suggest, of course, that there is not a need for more men but the machines come first.
There is also the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. llsley) with reference to the voluntary system, which appears on page 310 of Hansard:
I wish to say that neither as a member of the government nor as a member of the war committee of the cabinet, nor otherwise, have I been able to find any evidence that the abandonment of the voluntary system and the substitution of the compulsory system in respect to that part of our war effort represented by overseas army service would help at this moment in our war effort.
It is my opinion that we should be guided by our desire to serve, not only the people in our own ridings but the people of Canada as a whole. We are not being true to our duty if we sponsor legislation which might lead to disunity in this country even though such legislation might meet with the approval of our own people. Lord Tweedsmuir, speaking at Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island in September, 1937, and referring to the loyalty 44561-40t
of the Scottish people, not only to the land of their adoption but also to the land of their origin, said:
That is as it should be, for a man can never have too many loyalties. Therefore I want to see in the citizens of Canada strong and continuing love of the district to which they belong, but at the same time a strong and continuing interest in the dominion of which they are a part, the whole Canadian nation.
It is important that we should not become hysterical at a time such as this when we are faced with reverses. Reverses are inevitable in a war which is being fought on many fronts. I should like to quote from an editorial in the Globe and Mail of to-day. This refers to Prime Minister Churchill's reference to the difficulties we are facing and might expect to face in the future, and it says:
But these blows need not be mortal blows if we keep our heads and pursue our purpose relentlessly and with grim determination. That purpose is to convert our enormous potential power into an actual fighting force as rapidly as possible. We must build ships; produce aircraft; make guns; send the tanks rolling off the end of the production lines; and train men to operate these deadly engines.
Although we may be satisfied with our voluntary system as it is at the present time, and we have reason to be if we listen to those who are in charge, this attitude may change. I think it will change if the present system does not meet the emergencies that may arise. Should the system change, I am afraid there will be many difficulties in administration. We provide for compulsory service under the National Resources Mobilization Act, and even though this is confined to service in Canada, we have experienced many difficulties.
I believe hon. members who represent rural ridings will agree with me when I say that the majority of the requests received when we go home for week-ends are received from farmers' sons who are urging postponement of their military service. It is true that farmers have the privilege of asking for postponement, but I know of many cases where men have been taken away from large farms and no one left to operate them. I do not think postponement is sufficient. A farmer must plan, not only for months ahead but for years ahead. He must not be uncertain as to what he can do. He cannot plan if he knows that at any time he may be called into service and have to sell his farm and his stock. As I say, I think they should have more than postponement; they should have exemption in order that they can go ahead and plan for future operations.
There is some dissatisfaction with the procedure. If this is so in my constituency where the greatest distance from the district registrar
The Address-Mr. McCuaig

is only 100 miles, how much more is it so in areas where men are as far as 1,000 miles away from the divisional registrar? This is so in northern Ontario where the nearest registrar is in Toronto. There has been a dlemand that agriculture should be represented on these boards. Up to a short time ago the boards were made up of representatives of the Department of National Defence and the national labour supply council. This condition has been improved by the order in council passed on the seventh instant which provides that at the hearing of applications made to the board there shall also be a representative of agriculture in order that the interests of agriculture may be represented.
There also has been a demand for local boards which would ibe more familiar with the needs of the locality concerned. The argument against such boards is that there would be a danger that they might be influenced by representations made by people in the locality. If that argument is sound, then I suggest to the government that local committees be formed. These would not have administrative powers but would act merely as fact-finding bodies. These committees could be set up in each county or district, and they could forward the facts to the central board which would administer and deal with the application. In that way a committee need not be influenced because it could be said that they were merely a fact-finding body and were forwarding the facts to the board which was in charge of administration.
It is urged also that selective service should be extended to ail branches of our war effort, including the factory, the farm, as well as military service. I know the government is dealing with this problem, but we can readily see the difficulties in the way. This was brought out quite vividly on the tenth instant when the Minister of National Defence was speaking. He was referring to the policy of the government, and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) interrupted, as reported on page 452 of Hansard:	*
.	.	. is it anticipated that the government
intends to say to a man: "You shall work here and not there"? The Prime Minister has not made that clear. I do not think you can say to a man: "You must work here and not there". You might not get results.
Then, when the minister stated that this is receiving a great deal of examination and consideration in England as well as here, the leader of the opposition replied:
I am not sure that you can make a man work.
I would ask the government to give this policy their best consideration in the hope that some satisfactory arrangement may be made

in order to assure adequate help on the farm as well as in the factory. This might be accomplished by doing it indirectly, as is being done to a certain extent in the civil service, by refusing to hire a man in any industry if he is eligible for service or is better fitted for some other employment. In this regard some consideration must be given to the farmer as well as to those employed on the farm. A farmer under present market conditions cannot afford to pay' the wages received by those employed in industry and, on the other hand, it is not fair to the farm labourer to be compelled to work on the farm for wages much lower than he could receive were he allowed to work in industry. This problem, I am afraid, cannot be met in any way except by allowing the farmer to receive a higher reward for the commodities he produces.
Although there may be a difference of opinion as to the method by which the war is to be waged, I can assure the members of this house that my people are insistent that we should continue to prosecute the war to our utmost ability. I know the Minister of National Defence was speaking one hundred per cent for the people I represent when he said, as reported at page 448 of Hansard:
No person can doubt that Canada is committed to total war. We are committed to it not only for the survival of freedom generally but for our own survival and for the survival of this nation, and for the security of our own homes and families. To wage total war is the stated policy of the government and I believe, indeed I am sure, that it is the determined purpose of the Canadian people.
I will do all I can to urge the government to use every means at their disposal, including the conscription of wealth, if necessary, in order to wage total war, and I assure them that the people I represent are prepared to undergo any sacrifice requested of them. Let us all get behind the government in any move to increase the war effort, prod them on, if necessary, and show them the way by doing all we can to assist in the war loan, recruiting, the salvage campaign and the advancement of all organizations connected with our war effort; and, above all, let us remain united that we may hold this nation together in our struggle against the common foe.
Let me conclude with a quotation from the speech given by Prime Minister Churchill yesterday, when he said:
In the English-speaking world we rejoice in free institutions. We have free parliaments and a free press. This is the way of life we have been used to. This is the way of life we are fighting to defend.

The Address-Mr. Cloutier

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot conceal the emotion I feel on rising for the first time in this chamber to speak on behalf of the electors of Drummond-Arthabaska whom I have the honour to represent in the House of Commons since 1940. Though this emotion proceeds from various causes, I attribute it in great measure to the fact that Drummond-Arthabaska has been represented in the past by men of the first rank, and I wish I possessed the eloquence of Laurier, of Lavergne, of Dorion, or of Girouard, in order to give to the voice of my constituency the authority and competence it formerly had. Only a poet could do justice to my constituency, for Drummond-Arthabaska is certainly not an ordinary district. It is privileged in many respects. The soul of our national life is daily in evidence there, harmony reigns between the two races as among the various classes of society. Our farmers are performing real miracles on the land, and our workmen have not known even the shadow of the depression which has so seriously affected most urban centres.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, Drummond-Arthabaska has always been famous. This section of the country which is so dear to me has given great men to the nation, in the arts as well as in public life. Filled with national pride, my county has played a large part in the national war effort. At this moment my thoughts go to the brave defenders of Hong Kong, among whom many young heroes represent the contribution of Drummond-Arthabaska to the glorious Canadian army. Their sacrifice, like that of Dollard des Ormeaux and his valiant companions, will not have been in vain, and their glorious defeat is already worth more than a mere aureole of victory. They have displayed the tenacity of the Canadian soldier, his will to victory, his heroism. They are the symbol of a people which prizes freedom above all else and is ready to give everything, even life itself, to defend freedom until final victory.
I have every reason to be proud of my district, Mr. Speaker. It is admired by those who visit it and loved by those who live in it. With its vast plains recalling the western prairies, its delightful valleys, its poetic streams, its mountains characterized by beauty rather than loftiness, it is a miniature of Canada. Adolphe Poisson, whom Drummond-Arthabaska gave to French-Canadian literature, has sung the praises of this section of Canada in his immortal works, "Les heures perdues" and "Sous les pins." Inspired by the natural beauties of his native
district, he expressed sublime thoughts in harmonious verse.
And when admiring the illustrious works of the great sculptors Alfred Laliberte and Suzor Cote, we understand the scruples their chisels must have felt at hewing out masterpieces worthy of the grandeur and beauty of this bit of homeland.
And who is unaware of the renown of the enfant terrible of Drummond-Arthabaska, Erick Dorion, who brought to the politics of his time a note so ardent that even the enfant terrible of Temiscouata can hardly equal him to-day. I hope the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) will not mind this presumption on my part, for I shall tell him frankly, that, just as my electors, the men and women of Drummond-Arthabaska, I hold him in high admiration and consider him a great Canadian and an ardent patriot.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to pay a tribute to the memory of a man the centenary of whose birth was celebrated just a few months ago, the great statesman who was the pride of French Canada and the glory of the entire country, the man whom gracious Queen Victoria called "silver-tongued", Sir Wilfrid Laurier. We cherish with veneration numerous mementos of this great statesman who spent several of his finest years in the pleasant little town of Arthabaska and the village of l'Avenir, the home of Dorion, where he published a small newspaper which had considerable fame in its day. Drummond-Arthabaska will ever be proud of having had in its midst this great Canadian and illustrious patriot, a symbol of unity and an example of straightforwardness and justice towards all the races and' classes making up our beautiful country.
May I also, Mr. Speaker, associate myself with my fellow-members in paying a tender tribute to the memory of another great French Canadian, too early taken from our midst.
The people of Drummond-Arthabaska desire to pay a respectful tribute of admiration to the memory of the great patriot Ernest Lapointe. I feel that we shall miss him more and more in these troubled times. He was a man to whom we could turn in any emergency, and especially in time of peril. I hope that the policies of Laurier and of his successor Ernest Lapointe will ever be preserved by the Liberal party and that the life of those great statesmen will be an inspiration to all young Canadians. They embodied Canadian loyalty and patriotism.
I wish to tender my sincere * congratulations to the proposer (Mr. Fournier, Hull) and the seconder (Mr. Macdonald, Brantford City) of

The Address-Mr. Cloutier
the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They have discharged their task with dignity and expressed their views with courage.
I listened to their speeches with great interest and I admired the sincerity of their language.
I shall now discuss the six main points of the speech from the throne, considering them as much as possible from various angles. The first point is the proposed plebiscite concerning the use of our man-power. Mr. Speaker,
I understand that through such a plebiscite the government will request the people to release them from their past commitments as regards overseas military service. In my opinion it would have been preferable for the government to put directly to the electors the following question: "Are you for or against conscription for overseas service?" But since the government is asking the people whether they are in favour of releasing it from its pledge, I take both questions as being synonymous, even though the one that was selected may seem more ambiguous. I believe that such is the view of the people about the question of the plebiscite and they know that the future stand of the government will be either a wise one, in acordance with the policy they have followed so far, or a desperate, dangerous and useless course, according as the people reply in the negative or the affirmative to the question of the plebiscite.
The government was no doubt prompted by very grave reasons in deciding to consult the people. Besides, they promised, as I did myself in my constituency, that no momentous decision would be taken with regard to conscription without a plebiscite. For those reasons, I shall vote for the holding of a plebiscite, because I am a fervent Liberal and have the utmost confidence in my leaders.
But upholding as I do the policy inspired by Laurier and Lapointe, as well as by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) whom I greatly admire, I say once again that I am strongly opposed to conscription, and that I shall ever oppose with all my strength any compulsion for overseas service.
Nothing can justify such a policy, Mr. Speaker; of this I am convinced more than I could ever say. The voluntary system has given results of which Canada can be .proud. We have already supplied more troops than are needed by our allies. What is expected from us is first and above all material assistance. Ever since the beginning of the war, Canada has many times been referred to as the empire's arsenal. Our factories are work-

ing full time and they are supplying this country and our allies with weapons and munitions which may be a great contribution to final victory. Besides, we cannot as we did in 1914-18, be solely concerned with the defence of England and her possessions. Our shores are directly menaced by enemies who are drawing closer and closer to them. We are threatened with invasion from two directions. Our duty to Canada compels us to direct our energies, over and above all toward the defence of our own territory.
It would be the height of folly for us to carry our	friendship-undoubtedly	quite
legitimate-for England to the point of giving up too considerable a part of our armed forces. If we are to be attacked, a contingency which is considered possible and even probable, the assault will come as part of a general onslaught by our enemies, and on the same occasion England and the United States will have to oppose a fierce resistance against perfectly equipped enemies. We can only expect a rather -weak support from those allies, and to my mind it would be a mistake to believe that we can put all our strength into the defence of the empire while relying on help from our neighbours in a crisis. The most elementary prudence makes it imperative for us to attend first and above all to the defence of our own territory.
The tragic example of Australia should open our eyes. The Australians are now facing the terrible threat of an invasion by the Japanese and their army is no longer strong enough to withstand the attack easily.
The expected help is not forthcoming and not without emotion have we read their government's appeal and the words uttered by the venerable archbishop of Melbourne. Taking a leaf from such experience, I may say that if Britain, with its forty million people, cannot be everywhere at the same time and on every front, how can one expect Canada, with a population of eleven million, to set up a gigantic war production, supply large expeditionary forces and provide for its home defence at one and the same time? So. that, while I support the government on the plebiscite, I intend leaving my constituents perfectly free to cast their vote as they wish, without bringing any pressure to bear wrhatsoever, and as their conscience dictates. What result can we expect? Time will tell. If the answer is in the negative, I will ask the government not to interpret this as any lack of confidence. Quite the contrary, my constituents ardently wish to retain such a man as the Right Hon. Prime Minister at the head of affairs.

The Address-Mr. Harris (Grey-Bruce)
I still favour expeditionary forces raised on the basis of voluntary enlistment, but here again do I urge the wisdom of attending with greater care than ever to the maintenance of a sufficiently strong home force to meet such tragic and imminent dangers as now threaten our coasts. I am in accord with the government policy as regards the sending of arms and munitions to Britain. This constitutes the most valuable contribution we can offer and we must be generous in our aid to Great Britain that she may set up a military machine capable of ensuring the final overthrow of the axis' own machine.
I now come to the fourth outstanding feature of the speech from the throne: the extension of the government's policy of selective service and mobilization of our material and human resources to increase the national war effort. I have already stated my views on one aspect of mobilization. I must add here that the government's action in this domain should be dictated by the greatest prudence. I do wish the government would wholly share my views regarding agriculture and labour whose first duty is production to meet the nation's needs. Exemption from military service should apply to all farmers, farmers' sons and every one engaged in industrial pursuits related to agriculture, so as to provide our army and our population with all the necessaiy food. Exemption from military service should also be applied to those who are employed in munition plants and factories producing war supplies.
I agree that the largest possible number of Canadian citizens should be in a position to take up arms for the defence of the country in case of attack. Could1 we not, Mr. Speaker, organize in our towns and villages courses of preliminary training which farm and factory workers could attend without interfering with their productive tasks? By that I mean elementary military training given to farmers and factory workers after their working hours and in each locality. Uniforms would not be needed. It would simply be a matter of giving the elements of military training with a view to accustoming our people to handling arms, and to forming reserve battalions or guerilla troops for use in case of attack or invasion of the country.
Our worthy people would no doubt willingly devote a few hours a week to receiving an elementary training which might prove useful in the dark days this country may yet see.
I now come to the last point of the speech from the throne-the financing of the war. I am happy to note that Drummond^Arthabaska has done more than was asked of it in that domain. It is all to the credit of my electors,
and I am sure that Drummond-Arthabaska will continue in that patriotic path until the end of the conflict. My people want to purchase victory and I am sure such is the desire of all the citizens of Canada. In the face of the present danger it would be tragic and criminal parsimoniousness to count the dollars -that will bring victory. No matter how heavy the sacrifice, the people will respond generously to the call. Of that I am certain.
I shall be glad to vote with the government in favour of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, because it reflects above all the government's ardent desire to collaborate in a large way to the final victory of our arms.
In joyfully accepting all these sacrifices in a true spirit of national cooperation, we shall contribute to cementing the union of the two great races which compose our fair land and to make of Canada a country of two languages but a single heart.
