speechtext:
The address in reply to the speech from the throne has been very ably moved and seconded by the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Fournier) and the hon. member for Brantford City (Mr. Macdonald). Since that time there have been many very good speeches and much has been said; in fact little is left to be said. But on behalf of the riding I have the honour to represent I feel called upon to make a few remarks. It is customary, I believe, in the circumstances under which I rise also to say a few words about the riding itself.
Grey-Bruce is two-thirds rural. The urban part consists of towns and villages, none of which has a population of more than four thousand. The rural part is given over to mixed farming, particularly the raising of cattle, hogs and sheep and the production of butter. The counties of Grey and Bruce were first and third respectively in Ontario last year in the sale of butter, and they were among the first four in the sale of cattle, hogs and sheep. The urban part is mainly concerned with providing services for the farming communities and also with the manufacturing of furniture and similar wood products.
The people in the riding are almost entirely the descendants of the original settlers who came there between 1840 and 1880, and are from two main stocks, Anglo-Saxon and German. We have been very ably represented in public life; one of my predecessors from my home town distinguished himself in the chair which the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) now so graciously adorns and for whom the hon. member for Hull is at present an acceptable substitute. I might also add that in this house, in addition to the hon. member for
[	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Harris (Grey-Bruce)
Grey North (Mr. Telford), and the humble representative for Grey-Bruce, there are the following members who were born in the counties of Grey and Bruce: the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward), the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McNiven), the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), and the charming and hon. member for Edmonton East (Mrs. Casselman).
In this war the counties of Grey and Bruce are represented by three units: the 97th battery, mobilized in Walkerton in 1939, the 98th anti-tank battery mobilized July, 1940, in Port Elgin, and my own unit, the Grey and Simcoe Foresters, mobilized in June, 1940, as an infantry battalion as part of the 4th division.
All these units were raised with the minimum of delay, and enlistments have since been quite steady in the two counties. I cannot speak for the two batteries; but as far as my own unit is concerned, on those few occasions when by reason of medical discharges we went under strength there was no delay at all in getting recruits, they came almost overnight, as indeed they did on one occasion. Since that time, of course, there have been many enlistments in other branches of the army, in the navy and in the air force, and more recently there is recruiting going on for the two auxiliary women's organizations. In my unit, and in all the others, particularly perhaps the 97th battery, there is a large percentage of recruits from those areas which were settled by the original German immigrants. The young men of German racial origin in my counties have enlisted in quite as good percentage as the Anglo-Saxons.
The problems of the riding are naturally connected only with the war effort at the moment, and I should like to make a brief reference to the army, the navy and the air force.	.
The Canadian army which will be in existence at the end of this year, according to the plans of the government, will consist of whatever is overseas at the moment, plus the 4th division which in the meantime will have become armoured. The Canadian army will then consist of two corps: the first, of three infantry divisions with two army tank brigades attached; and the second, of two armoured divisions. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) was, I thought, rather modest when he referred to the Canadian army as it will be; he said it would be at least equal to anything in the armed forces of the empire, as I recall the phrase. But I should like to point out that Germany is popularly supposed to have invaded France

with eleven armoured divisions out of sixty, and to have invaded Russia with twenty armoured divisions out of one hundred or one hundred and twenty. In neither case was the percentage of armoured units equal to the two out of five which the Canadian army will have on completion of this year's plan.
I might say that the feeling of the riding is not only commendation of the fact that the Canadian army will be self-contained and self-directed, but it is considered essential that that should be so.
With respect to the navy, we have had enlistments from our counties, and unfortunately there have been losses, which we all regret. Nevertheless the work of the navy was rather remote from the people of my riding until my battalion went east last spring, and the members of the unit began to see the navy in action and to see the difficulties with which it contends.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that the fact that the Canadian navy has grown from 15 to 350 ships and now has a personnel of
27,000	is not only commendable but laudable; yet, knowing the battle of the Atlantic and of Great Britain as we do now, and in view of the situation which has resulted from the withdrawal of at least part of the United States navy to the Pacific, in my opinion it must be the first duty of this government not only to continue the shipbuilding programme which has brought about that great increase, but to extend it and to continue to extend it for many months to come. The battle of the Atlantic has not even been won at the moment, though it has not been lost; and until our production of ships has run away ahead of our losses for some time, we cannot afford to take any risks on the danger with which we have been faced during the past two years..
With respect to the air force, of course we are familiar with that because of the large number of enlistments from my riding, and the fact that the Canadian government will spend something like 8800,000,000 on the British commonwealth air training plan shows the importance of this project. But here again, in my opinion, the plan, while a great one, is not yet sufficient for the needs of the Dominion of Canada. It is heartening, of course, to learn that the number of recruits entering the training centres of the air force monthly has been quite sufficient, but that is sufficient according to the yardstick which we followed some months ago. Surely it is evident to every one in this house that in no engagement so far in this war has t'he side without air strength succeeded in winning. Therefore not only should the number of

The Address-Mr. Harris (Grey-Bruce)
recruits be increased, but the plan itself should be broadened so that in the near future planes and pilots will be available in much greater numbers than we now have them.
I suppose the house would expect me to make some reference to the munitions programme. I must confess that the figures as to contracts granted and amounts of money involved are beyond my comprehension. But the figures of production do mean something to me, and I wonder whether we are not under a misapprehension about them. I do not say that in an endeavour to reflect in any manner upon the government, but some hon. members and some speakers are prone to make reference to the percentage of our production now in comparison with what it was in our first, unprepared condition. I hope that in making its plans for this year the government will bear in mind not what we did last year, but what Hitler and his allies are doing this year. Our production should be aimed to overtake that production, and no other yardstick should be used.
When we met some twenty months ago, all hon. members were acutely aware of our shortage of war equipment, and we had a rather gloomy outlook. But I am afraid we have forgotten that, to the extent that we have overlooked not only the production which Hitler had on hand at that time, but what he has been able to accumulate since. He has had the productive capacity of Europe, with the exception of Russia and Great Britain, since that time. However, 1941 did give us one very considerable stroke of good luck, shall I say. Hitler attacked Russia, and since then he has lost a large number of men and a large amount of equipment, while on our side we have gained a large number of men and a large amount of equipment from Russia. Similarly, we have lost the manpower and the productive capacity of Japan, but we have gained those of the United States. With all this, however, it is my opinion, as I think it is the opinion of my riding, that the production of this country should be greatly expanded before we undertake any great expansion of our armed forces. I understand, from figures given the other night by the Minister of National Defence, that at present there are 600,000 people in the dominion engaged directly or indirectly in the production of munitions and war equipment, and that another 100,000 will be added this year. I must say this is a large number. Yet it is not anything like what we can have and what we should have as the facilities increase.
As I pointed out a short time ago, in my county there have been many enlistments in
all branches of the armed services. This has brought about a shortage of farm labour; and while the farmer himself is as willing as anyone to suffer inconvenience and loss in the prosecution of the war, he knows that food is necessary in Great Britain to-day; he knows that it will be necessary next year, and he knows that at the end of the war we should have a surplus on hand for the purpose of feeding the millions who will be starving in Europe at that time. Having all this in mind, he finds it hard to understand, in some cases at least, the drain on labour from the farm, not only into the armed forces but into munition factories and other more gainful employment in the cities. In my opinion this situation should be corrected this year, and I was glad to see that in his speech the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made reference to it, which reference I shall give in a few moments.
In addition to the farmers, other civilians in my riding have been under the impression that they have not yet done anything like what they could and should do in the prosecution of the war. They have engaged in successful salvage campaigns; they have participated in the war loans; they have bought war savings certificates and stamps; they have engaged in Red Cross and similar activities, but at the same time they still think they could do a great deal more. They agree that the changeover from a peaceful nation into one with a war economy cannot be done overnight. They agree also that the government, with all due respect to some hon. members opposite, has laid a very good foundation for our war effort, and they agree that the future will see an orderly and effective advance to an all-out effort. But with all that, they do feel that now, the foundation having been laid, something more could be done by them and, further, they believe it is the duty of the government to provide that opportunity. I am glad to say that the Prime Minister has been ahead of me in this also, and in his speech made some reference to it. With the permission of the house I shall read these references now, because they apply to both farmers and civilians. Those words appear at pages 45 and 46 of Hansard for Monday, January 26:
The government now proposes to apply the compulsory powers of national selective service to other aspects of the war effort as well as to military service. These powers will be applied selectively and progressively to those activities where it is considered by the government that their application will contribute to the goal of a total effort. ...
I shall not attempt at this time to outline the measures which are contemplated in order to extend the scope of national selective service. I shall confine myself to saying that the extended policy of selective service will com-
626	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Harris (Grey-Bruce)
prebend measures to increase the supply of man-power available for war industry and for the armed forces; also measures to safeguard and, where necessary, to assist in providing agricultural labour required to expand war production on the farm. These objects it is proposed to achieve by positive action to increase the mobility of available man-power, to add to the number of women available for employment, and to facilitate the transfer of labour from non-essential occupations to direct employment in the furtherance of the war effort.
I am naturally concerned with the present and future condition of the soldier, sailor and airman, to whom I shall refer hereafter only as soldiers. I was not satisfied that the condition of soldiers' dependents last year was what it should be, in view of the increased incomes of the civilian population, particularly in Ontario, and probably other parts of the dominion. To the soldier who went home on week-end leave it was quite evident that the civilian population were spending large sums of money on pleasures, and with respect to other matters which, at best, were luxuries. It was unfortunate for that soldier to meet the person-the young man or the young lady -who took his particular position in civilian life, because the civilian occupying the position vacated by the soldier was in all cases found to be earning considerably higher than had the soldier at the time of enlistment. In view of this I was in favour of increasing the allowance for the dependents of soldiers, and of increasing soldiers' pay, up to and including the rank of warrant officer. I hope the house will understand that neither my wife nor my children are in receipt of allowances, so that anything I may say is quite unbiased in that respect.
Nevertheless the government decided to institute trustee boards to which applications could be made by dependents, to show that they had special cases where greater allowance was required. I do not agree with this system, may I say with all respect to those who brought it about. The cost of living mounted very sharply in Ontario, at least during the twelve months of 1941, and cost of living bonuses were provided for many types of wage-earners. They were not, however, provided for soldiers. The price ceiling was placed upon nearly everything, if not everything, and the cost of living since that time has remained relatively constant. Therefore I now suggest to the government that with the cost of living well under control, the dependents' allowance might be increased by a flat rate, and that such action would not require the assistance of the trustee boards which have been set up. However competent they may be, they will make mistakes. And there will be some cost 
in connection with the machinery, no matter how much it is kept down by the government itself, and by those individuals who are willing to serve on it.
The disparity between the earning power of the soldier and the civilian is common to all wars, and I do not suppose it can be adjusted adequately to suit the soldier. At the same time there are benefits received by the soldier upon his return, and I believe I should place them on record. If the soldier is discharged for medical reasons, he receives free hospitalization; and if he is in a civilian hospital, he and his dependents receive some allowance while he is there. If he is discharged for other reasons at the conclusion of the war, and if he has been in the army for a period of six months, he receives, in addition to the clothing allowance, one month's pay and allowance, and he also receives free treatment in the department's hospitals for twelve months for anything which may occur during that time.
In addition to this, he receives his old job back, if he wishes to have it. I am pleased' to say the government is changing this provision from the order in council which has existed for some months, into a bill already before the house. If, however, he was not employed when he enlisted, or if for any reason he does not wish his old job back, if single he receives S9 a week and, if married, $13 a week, for a limited period' of time while seeking employment. He also receives training in some type of employment he may choose and, in addition, he is in receipt of the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act. If, as happens so often, he leaves his education uncompleted in order to join the army, he receives free tuition, and' a modest living allowance while he completes his course. These are substantial benefits, and go a long way toward placing a soldier back where he started when he enlisted.
However, from my slight experience in the army-and this is a point which, I am sure, is appreciated by all hon. members who are returned men-I believe that nothing which can be done by the house can place the soldier back in the position he was in when he enlisted, whether his service in the army has been for only three or four months, or for two or three years. Therefore any consideration given by hon. members to provision for veterans of this war as well as those of the last will, I hope, be given with that point in mind. Nothing we can do will adjust those men completely to their previous civil status.
After what happened a week ago, I should not think it necessary to make any reference to the plebiscite. My silence might, how-

The Address-Mr. Blanchette
ever, be misconstrued, ar>d perhaps I ought to make some brief observations. I am quite in favour of holding the plebiscite, partly because I believe it the right thing to do in any event, and partly for personal reasons. In my own riding 'I stated the policy of the Liberal party, as I understood it, in these words:
The Liberal party is opposed to conscription for overseas service, but we are pledged to prosecuting the war with the utmost vigour, short of that.
Those are the words which I used., and which were reported in the local press. Under those circumstances I would find it quite impossible to come to the house and discuss the question; I would 'be limited to my promise made during the election campaign. Since it seems that conscription will be discussed, probably debated at length in the house in coming months, I would wish to be free so that 'I might take my part in that discussion.
It seems to me that there will be three classes of persons who will vote on the plebiscite. First there will be the person in favour of conscription for overseas service; he will vote in the affirmative. Then there is the person opposed under all circumstances to conscription for overseas service; he will vote in the negative. Then there will be the third person-and in my view this will be the largest group-who has no settled conviction one way or another, but who is willing to vote "yes", and leave the decision to the .government which so far has guided the country successfully through two years of -war. I am pleased that the plebiscite is being taken, and1 that the government has said that with the utmost vigour it would see that the question is fairly put to the people, and that an affirmative answer will be requested of the electorate.
In conclusion, perhaps I may be permitted to make a few observations respecting the soldiers with whom I have been associated for twenty months. I would remind hon. members that Hitler has said he is fighting against democracy. We tell our soldiers we are fighting for democracy. To a member of the armed forces democracy is not an abstract thing, nor is it necessarily the best form of government. Many of our men have no opinion on the point at all-nor could they be expected to have. But democracy to them is that form of government we have in Canada, the form we are fighting to maintain. We fight for it because it is our choice, and for no other reason. Under these circumstances, while democracy in the abstract may mean nothing to the soldier, the deliberations -of this house do mean something. They are
reported in the newspapers and are familiar to all ranks. The standard of our public life should be maintained with that in mind. I ask the house to remember that in this session and in all sessions until the war is over it is essential, not only that everything that happens here should be directed to winning the war, but that nothing be said in this house to detract from the symbol for which the armed forces are fighting.
Persons in and outside the house have at times made references to persons in the house and in authority, and to others who enjoy the confidence of the electorate which go a long way toward destroying the honour which is due to this house and to the members of it. We are expecting the armed forces to fight for us as an institution. They are willing to do that, but they expect that this house will conduct itself in a manner befitting the sacrifice they are making. I do not intend to say anything more along this line.
In all probability some time during this year, or next year, the Canadian army will proceed to the scene of conflict. They will be convoyed in British and Canadian ships, manned by Canadian sailors, guarded overhead by the Canadian air force. When that time comes we must see, not only that our soldier is well trained but that his equipment is adequate and superior in quality and quantity to the enemy's; we must be able to assure him that behind him there is a civilian population whose morale is as good as his, so that when he faces the greatest task he will be able to meet the Germans and their allies and defeat them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I desire to add my congratulations to those expressed already to the mover (Mr. Fournier, Hull), and the seconder (Mr. Macdonald, Brantford City) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I desire also, on behalf of the county of Compton, to congratulate the Minister of Justice, Mr. St. Laurent. The minister was born in the county of Compton in the eastern townships, where, as he himself has stated, he learned to speak French to his father and English to his mother. In many respects he thus became a true exponent of the eastern townships.
At this late stage of the debate it would be imposing upon the indulgence of this hon. house were I to bring up again what has been said already by hon. members on the subjects of conscription and the plebiscite. In my remarks this evening my intention is not to go into the various details of the matter under discussion but rather to treat both these subjects in a general way, based

The Address-Mr. Blanchette
upon what has been advanced in this house as well as out of it. I intend to mention the Hong Kong matter and to speak briefly on social legislation.
On September 8, 1939, when I had the honour of seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I stated, as reported on page 12 of Hansard:
I wish to state, without the slightest hesitation and without any mental reservation, that I am fully opposed to conscription. I am completely against a system so inconsistent with our Canadian turn of mind. Experience has shown moreover that it is not effective, for, without having given the desired results, it has, in the past, fostered trouble and unsettled our national life.
In order, therefore, that none may falsely construe my attitude in the matter, I repeat that I am completely opposed to conscription.
During the election in the following year, 1940, I repeated that assertion throughout the length and breadth of my constituency. The result was that the majority I received at that time was greater by one hundred per cent than the largest majority ever given any candidate in the history of the constituency of Compton. In making this statement I attribute no credit to myself. It is due rather to the present leader of the government whose programme was endorsed by the electors of my constituency. My conviction upon the subject of conscription is still the same. I feel that conscription is unnecessary, that it would undermine our national unity and that in having recourse to it we would defeat the very aim we have in view, that is, a total war effort. Since the declaration of war by this country, we have had practically at all times a sufficient number of volunteers whom we could clothe and equip and train. Recently we had figures from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) to the effect that total voluntary enlistments in January of this year were 18,285, broken down as follows:
Navy	 800
Army	 11,713
Air force	   5,772
I should like to quote the words of the Minister of National Defence, to be found on page 455 of Hansard of this year, as follows:
You can hardly say, Mr. Speaker, that the voluntary system has failed. Let us not forget that these enlistments have come not under the patriotic fervour which casualties produces, but at a time when because of comparative inactivity it was naturally harder to convince our people that the army needed men. We at national defence headquarters are going right on, and I ask most sincerely for the active interest of the members of this house and of the citizens generally to back up our efforts.
In his address to his men General McNaughton stated that this government had

done all that it possibly could do in the way of an efficient effort in the war. Prime Minister Churchill, Lord Beaverbrook and others who have visited us from Great Britain have declared that our effort is magnificent. With Great Britain attacked as she has been I feel that it would have been treason on their part to assert this if they were not convinced it was the truth. I feel that these testimonials from responsible persons who ought to know should take precedence over the wails, lamentations and deprecations of our backseat driving, shall I say, journalistic or paper generals. I feel that if these generals would only spend as much of their time in giving an impulse to voluntary enlistments as they have done and are doing for conscription, there never would be any doubt as to the results obtained in the future with our voluntary system of enlistment. In so doing they will be logical and sincere in the aim which they assume, namely, the supplying of all the men that are needed for an all-out war effort.
Let us not lose sight of the fact, Mr. Speaker, that our population consists of only eleven and a half million people, and that up to the end of 1941 we had already in the Canadian service over 500,000 men, of whom
422.000	have volunteered. In addition, according to plans laid out by the Department of National Defence, as set out at page 450 of Hansard, with additional recruits this year of from 173,000 to 193,000, we shall have over
700.000	under military arms. That is more than six per cent of our total population, which would represent, according to population, armies of the following size for some of our allied countries:
Russia	 10,800,000
United States	 7,800,000
United Kingdom	 3,000,000
Union of South Africa	 600,000
Australia and New Zealand....	600.000
British empire in Africa	 2,700,000
British empire in Asia	 24,000,000
Netherlands in East Indies		4.200,000
China	 27,000,000
The New York Times in its issue of yesterday, February 15, states in its editorial:
An armed force of 7,000,000 (for the United States) is within reason. There can hardly be more than that number if we take official estimates of 15 or 20 civilian workers for each man under arms.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, if the United States with its population of 130 millions and its mass production recognizes officially that not more than six per cent should be placed under arms, can we outdo and outbid the United States in our efforts to enlist manpower?
I am one of those who firmly believe that our voluntary system has worked well in the

The Address-Mr. Blanchette
recruiting of our man-power, and I feel that the government would be egregiously wrong in resorting to some other method.
That conscription would have a disquieting effect upon this country is plain to those who have eyes to see and ears to hear. In spite of the opinions which we might have to the contrary, the experience of the last war is there to prove it.
I know that there are some who make light of this term, "national unity," calling it a red herring, a bogy. We have heard those very terms and qualifications used in this house, and as a rule those who make the most pronounced charges in that sense show at present, as they have shown in the past, that, to say the best, their actions do not always tend toward national unity. Incidentally I might state that the Conservative party by its conscription propaganda has forced out of its ranks the only representative it had from the province of Quebec. No, Mr. Speaker, the success of our war effort, spoken of in such laudable terms by those outside Canada, but detracted from, to put it mildly, by a certain stentorian group in this country, has been possible only because of the success in maintaining national unity; and the moment that unity is scuttled, arrested or defeated, I shall fear for our total war effort in this war, as I would fear also for our peace effort after the war. Surely, if the fathers of confederation were able to adjust their differences in their day to make us a united nation, can it be thought that we, the sons of confederation, have so retrogressed in the realm of love of country and all that it means to us, have moved so far back to pre-confederation years, that we can no longer maintain united this young nation of ours? Unity is the result of adjusted differences; disunity represents uncompromised differences.
Everyone in this country has the same end in view, the winning of the war. The difference is only one of means to attain that end. I confess that the case might be hopeless if the end to be arrived at were disputed by anyone in this country, which it is not; and surely we can agree on the means to arrive at our objective. The war front is only as strong and as effective as the home front; the one is the necessary complement of the other. In war neither one of these fronts can continue alone if one is impaired in unity and efficiency.
What we have accomplished to date in finance, in the enlistment of man-power and in production has been done for the most part, be it noted, by voluntary methods. These, Mr. Speaker, are my humble views upon conscription, which I believe is unnecessary and would disunite this country and defeat our efforts to attain the very goal at which we are aiming.
But equally as contentious as conscription is the plebiscite proposal in the speech from the throne. This popular consultation, as I see it, represents, to me at least, the quintessence of democracy. I am one of those who have faith in the people. I believe they will pronounce according to the dictates of their mind and conscience in the matter; and is not the free expression of the people, according to their dictates, exactly what this country and all the other democracies are fighting for to-day

freedom of mind in the affairs of religion, freedom of expression in the affairs of state, all of which are advance posts of democracy?
The plebiscite is not a pronouncement on conscription. It is a release from the promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as well as by practically seventy-five per cent of the members of this house who were elected at the last election, a promise made by both leaders of the two major parties at the last election. But there is this to be noted, that whereas the Prime Minister asked for release from his promise, and that from the whole people of Canada, the new leader of the Conservative party, in spite of the promise in the same sense that was made by his party at the last election, relegated that promise to the four winds immediately upon -I shall not say his election or choice by the Tory party-but rather upon his appointment by a certain group in the country. Is it not more democratic to follow the course our Prime Minister has taken and have recourse to the popular will rather than to decide arbitrarily of one's own accord that an engagement shall be broken and that in spite of the promises made by Mr. Meighen in 1925, which he made first in Ontario when he stated at Hamilton:
I have myself not the slightest fear but that, if danger threatened Canada again, this country would respond as it responded in 1914; but I believe that in future it will be best for all that before a government takes a step so momentous as the dispatch of troops, the will of the people should be known.
Again, a few days later, in Acton Vale, Quebec, during the course of a by-election in the county of Bagot, the new leader of the Tory party spoke as follows:
If a crisis should occur in which our country's peace would be threatened, I declare, so long as the reins of power are in my hands-I declare this country will not send a man out of Canada without the country being consulted.
In other words, the present leader of the Conservative party believes in popular consultation on the subject when he is in power,
The Address-Mr. Blanchette

but is totally against it when not in power. I feel that we can exact, and we must exact, of our public men precisely the same standard of integrity, honesty and probity in the pledged word as we expect in our common daily relations with our fellow men.
Once again, I am of opinion that the plebiscite is a democratic measure, and I do not feel that the severe criticism upon this measure is justified. I am glad to note that during the debate which has been progressing there is at least one point upon which we all seem to be unanimous, and that is the common assertion that the Department of National War Services should do all within its power, by its different boards throughout the country, to enable agriculture to carry on, in the adjournments of military training for farmers' sons. We have had instances of that this evening. Practically every member who spoke made recommendations in that sense-the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. McCuaig), the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Gladstone), the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Harris), the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Cloutier), for instance; and I am only too glad to associate myself with the sentiments which they have expressed in that regard.
In many instances the call of farmers' sons for military training puts in danger the continuation of the farm, and I would suggest that all possible consideration be accorded such demands. In expressing this view I am only conveying to the house the text of many petitions which I have received, and which all hon. members have received, in that connection. The carrying on of agriculture on a larger scale than ever is of equal importance with the making of munitions and equipment, and I am of opinion that everything should be done to exempt farmers' sons from military training.
There is, however, one point to which I would call the attention of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), and that is the case of farmers' sons who are at present doing military training in camps-this because the recruit did not make his representations in time, or for other exceptional reasons, the result being that he is called anyway. There are a number of such cases in my constituency, and I find that the procedure is unreasonably slow to get such men out of the training camps and to bring them back to the farms, where they are more useful to the country and to our allies.
I sincerely endorse the decision of the government to have an immediate inquiry into the disaster of Hong Kong, with a view to imposing the necessary sanction upon those

responsible for this calamity, in order that this inquiry may serve as a lesson to anyone in high command who unnecessarily takes an unsound and unreasonable attitude toward the lives of the men. I do not believe any *county in the eastern townships has furnished more men for the Hong Kong organization than did Compton, where men were recruited in large numbers from such centres as Bury, Scotstown, Cookshire, Sawyerville, Island Brook, East Angus, Lake Megantic and other localities of the riding.
Needless to say, the news of the fall of Hong Kong brought a great deal of sorrow to a very large portion of my constituents, and I know the sympathy of the country goes out to them and to their fallen heroes. With *bowed heads at all times, let us always remember their deeds of valour and their supreme sacrifice.
I would not be true to the convictions which I hold did I not say a word on this occasion with regard to social legislation, too little of which we have heard for a number of years past, compared with European countries. I have already introduced in this house a measure for subsidizing large families; and although I do not believe that this measure, if put into effect, would result in an increase in the size of our families, I feel that such a step would greatly assist such families in the proper bringing up of their children from the *point of view of proper nourishment and health, among many other advantages that would result. Had we had this legislation in the past, who is there that can deny that we might have to-day two or three hundred thousand more hands to turn the wheels of industry and to carry on our farms, as well as men in our training camps-a wealth of which we have been deprived by premature deaths or undernourishment among those who fill our hospitals to-day as a result of lack of assistance given this human capital?
The eminent sociologist, Doctor Eleanor E. Rathbone, has truly said that children are not simply a private luxury; they are an asset to the community, and the community can no longer afford to leave provision for their welfare solely to the accident of individual incomes. The Right Rev. Dean Williams, Archbishop of Huron, speaking on this subject said that the best way to populate the vacant spaces of Canada is to populate them with the children of Canada; and the fallowing words are from Mr. Justice Powers, President of the Commonwealth Arbitration Court of Australia:
Family allowances will, if adopted, remove
the greatest cause of industrial discontentment and misery, namely, the inability of many

The Address-Mr. Mills
workers to feed their children properly and clothe them decently, however hard they work for their basic wage.
In a radio broadcast address the Rev. Father S. J. Lebel, S.J., the eminent sociologist, truly stated:
All governments have a duty to make a very serious study of family allocation. It is one of the most pressing questions of the hour. Upon its solution is dependent in large measure that true social peace and the real prosperity of the dominion.
There exists a common relation between the family and the state, a relation such that whatever contributes to the welfare and strength of the family, also contributes to the welfare and strength of the state. All that is indispensable to the family is also indispensable to the state. In spite of the seriousness of the hour, with its pain and suffering, Great Britain has already been seized with the importance of this legislation and has already submitted to its parliament a study of this important question of family allocation. I cannot too strongly urge the present government to take a step in the same direction in order that the proper orientation be given to this legislation as something that will greatly help this country and add to its- war strength, at the same time granting the blessings of distributive justice. We speak of a new order to follow the war; let us not believe that this new order will arrive with the break of day some fine morning; we must begin to break the shackles of the old if we wish to prepare for the new. By all means let us slave and save and sacrifice to win the war, but let us sacrifice and save and slave also to win social peace after the war.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In rising to add a word in this debate on the address, I am not going to repeat what has already been said by handing bouquets to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, who both did justice to the honour assigned to them.
I have the honour to represent the pioneer county of Elgin, Ontario, noted and outstanding in many ways. The county is ideally located on the north shore of lake Erie; St. Thomas, my county town, is midway between Fort Erie and Windsor on No. 3 highway, a shortcut for United States travellers across Ontario. St. Thomas is the Canadian terminal for three great railways; the New York Central, the Wabash and the Pere Marquette. The shops of the New York Central are located there, and the Pere Marquette have new shops almost completed. We also have the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian National and the London and Port Stanley railways, the latter, I believe, being the last remaining
electric road running across country. Therefore St. Thomas is rightly called the railway city.
St. Thomas has also the most outstanding, up-to-the-minute daily newspaper in Canada. The editor of that paper, after reading the speech from the throne, gave St. Thomas world-wide publicity by cabling to the Right Hon. Winston Churchill and telegraphing President Roosevelt and headlining on the front page the following message:
Canadians feel humiliated and apologize for action of their premier in proposing plebiscite on military service, believing it falsely represents them as failing to realize gravity of situation and necessity of all-out effort to save themselves and empire. Believe unparalleled circumstances require that you should create precedent and advise Mackenzie King to abandon idea and take only step possible for utmost prosecution of war without delay.
I have been following the paper looking for a reply, but so far the only reply I have seen is where in the British parliament Prime Minister Churchill gave an account of the great contribution Canada has made to the war and the great applause his statement received.
Elgin is a great agricultural county, producing great quantities of 'hogs, beans, beef cattle, tobacco, small fruits, milk and, of course hon. members all know, the finest apples in the world.
The government, of which I am proud to be a supporter, has located in Elgin county several airports in connection with the commonwealth air training plan. Three miles south of St. Thomas was the great new Ontario mental hospital. The provincial government immediately on the outbreak of the war, turned that hospital over to the Department of National Defence. The technical training school in connection with the air training plan is now located in Elgin county, and between 5,000 and 6,000 men are stationed there all the time. Then we have the Fingal bombing and gunnery school with a personnel of 1,200 to 1,500, also Aylmer air school for pilots with about the same personnel. They have almost completed an emergency landing field five miles east of St. Thomas and needless to say, St. Thomas and Elgin county have been stimulated to great activity by reason of these training centres. We are grateful to the government for locating them there. Then we have at Port Stanley the finest harbour on the north shore of lake Erie, being the lake port for St. Thomas and London and also the home of a great fishing industry.
Last, but not least, Elgin county is the 'home of the best known provincial premier in Canada, in the person of Hon. Mitchell Hepburn. Mitchell is always putting Elgin county
The Address-Mr. Mills

on the map. Our friendship dates back to long before either of us entered public life. We have a standing agreement; Mitch grows my onions and I grow his apples. Mitch has always given me his loyal support, and I shall always do likewise any time he appeals to the electors of Elgin county.
As to the government, one might write a book on their accomplishments in the last seven years. I have not time to dwell at any length on them, but in passing let me say that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is the only outstanding statesman and leader in Canada to-day. He is surrounded by the best ministers it is possible to get. Where in Canada could you better our three ministers of national defence? Where in Canada could you better our Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe)? Who has any fault to find with any of them? We have the most representative national government possible, a government representing more parts of Canada than any government since confederation.
I have no time to go into the benefits and accomplishments of this government since it came into power, but let me just touch on the Prime Minister's ability. For example, immediately after he was elected he negotiated a trade treaty with the United States. I shall mention just one benefit from this trade agreement, in reference to cattle. We have in our stables a great many beef cattle, and therefore I know something about what I am saying. We are allowed a quota of about 52,000 head of cattle over 700 pounds each, entering the United States every three months, at one and a half cents a pound duty. The quota which started in January was filled in about six weeks. This makes a grand market for our cattle. What would our cattle market be like at the present time, with no export to Britain, if it were not for this agreement, which Lord Bennett, as he now is, tried three years to negotiate but without success?
A great deal is owing to our Prime Minister for the great cooperation between Great Britain, the United States and Canada to-day. My. opponent, speaking in St. Thomas on February 14, 1940, at the last election, six months after war was declared, was criticizing a Liberal poster which read1: "Forward with Mackenzie King". He said, "Forward; where to?" Answering his own question he said, "To closer relationships with the United States." I wonder whether he would make such a statement to-day. I doubt if our Conservative friends will ever again choose as an election slogan, "No truck or trade with the Yankees." I have always advocated close relationships with the United States. Why not? Many of our sons and daughters are permanently settled1 there.
 '
Canada's war effort has been fully explained by previous speakers, so there is no need for me to repeat what has been said. But let me refer to an editorial in the New York Times, which said that Canada's contribution is one of the miracles of the war, according to her population.
As I see it, the situation is that, as time goes on, Canada will almost become the cupboard of the world. A few days ago I was reading an article on conditions in Europe, where thousands are cold and hungry. Will Canada soon not have to be sending food supplies to Russia as well as England? Canadian farmers are as loyal and patriotic as any people we have in Canada. They have met the demands made upon them and are willing to continue working long hours and doing their best, but they are becoming greatly handicapped by the labour situation. The calling up of men as recruits for the training centres, the employment of men by factories, shops and the railways, make it almost impossible to hire men for farm work. The only farmer who is going to get by is the small farmer, who can do the work himself.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I come to the question of calling up young farmers for war service. The procedure under the present policy is very unsatisfactory. First let me say that Mr. W. A. Martin, the divisional registrar at London, who represents the whole of western Ontario, is the finest, fairest type of man it would be possible to have in that position. He wants to be fair and impose no hardship on anyone, but he has an impossible task; no one man can act as a tribunal for all western Ontario. I should like to give my experience only a short time ago. About ten o'clock in the morning I called his office. The long-distance operator reported back that Mr. Martin could not talk to me until after two o'clock. I said to her, "I will not be sitting at this telephone at two o'clock. You tell him W. H. Mills wants to speak to him, and I think he will speak to me." I was talking to him inside of a minute. If it had been a farmer from a back concession who had called, there would have been some other alibi at two o'clock because his staff simply have to protect him. He cannot attend personally to all the demands made upon him.
I should now like to mention my experience in interceding in one or two cases, although I could refer to many. A short time before I came to Ottawa, a lady and her son came to see me one evening. I found that she was a widow, with one son and a married daughter. The son was the only help she had. They came to see me on New Year's day, and the

The Address-Mr. Mills
son. had been notified to report at the Chatham training camp the following Thursday, which would leave no one to do the work.
I should like to read one paragraph from the letter I wrote to Mr. Martin in this connection:
He is the only son of a widowed mother. She has one daughter who is married and away from home. They have one hundred and ninety acres of land, fourteen milch cows, sending the milk to the Corinth cheese factory, fourteen young cattle, four brood sows, turning off approximately forty to fifty hogs a year, have four horses, and do general farming. Wilford has been doing the work on this farm alone with no hired man and it is out of the question to get one. If he has to take this four-month training, there would be nothing else but a sale and quit farming. At this late date, it is even too late to have a sale in time, and they do not want to do this anyway. It is not the intention of the department that a widow's only son should have to go into training and the farm be abandoned. The Hon. James Gardiner spoke especially on this point at the London meeting a year ago.
I asked Mrs. Burwell at what time they got their mail, and she said, "About nine o'clock in the morning." So I said, "If you do not hear anything by next Tuesday as a result of the letter I will write, you telephone me and I will telephone Mr. Martin." Then I added, "You go home, go to bed, and get some sleep," because I could see that she was greatly worried. I added, "You take it from me, Wilford is not going into training next Thursday." I heard nothing more for some time, so I took it that they had received the looked-for letter. Then Mrs. Burwell sent me a copy of a letter they had received giving her son a postponement until March 31, a date not far off now. If she took that letter too much to heart, she still would not be sleeping nights because the letter said that Wilford would be expected to report at the first training camp after that date, and that he would be notified in ample time as to the place and date.
I contend that there should be some different policy from this worrying of widowed mothers. I would refer to another case, that of a young man who finished his four months' training last July, was given a postponement for six months and then was notified to return to duty on December 15. Prior to that date he and his father interviewed me to see if something could not be done, so I wrote a letter in his behalf to the commander in charge, Wolseley barracks, where he was sitpposed to report. -This young man's father, Mr. Danbrook, has only one other son, who has been in the 'air force for over a year and a half. The other boy, Keith, is married and lived at home with his father, working the farm with him. They have two hundred
acres-I know the farm very well-twenty-two Holstein cows and sixteen young cattle, an accredited herd. They kept hogs until some time ago, when they had an outbreak of hog cholera and their twenty-six hogs were slaughtered, but they are going back into hogs shortly, and are carrying on general farm work. This boy went to London, without result, and he was instructed to report at the barracks. I wrote the commander there, and received this reply:
This young lad has reported here for duty and is at the present moment being held in the depot for disposal.
I regret that I am unable to take any steps regarding any further postponement but would suggest that you write the district officer commanding, headquarters, M.D. No. 1, London, who will issue instructions to me as to what disposal I am to make of this young man.
I wrote as suggested, enclosing a copy of the letter I had written to the commander at Wolseley barracks, and saying I could add nothing more except that the father was confined to bed at that time with a paralysed shoulder. Then I got the following acknowledgment from him:
This man has completed his four-months training as a reserve recruit and has now automatically become a member of the Canadian army "home defence".
Had he applied to the Department of National War Services prior to 15th December it is possible that he might have secured an additional postponement, but now his status is the same as a member of the Canadian army active.
We have had this man in and suggested to him that it is thought that he might possibly secure a discharge on compassionate grounds, and further suggested that he should forward an application through his commanding officer for a discharge.
The next information I received was in a letter from his father. They had a neighbour boy helping to do the chores, and the son was sent to Camp Borden to wash dishes. He remained there for about three weeks, and then finally, on January 14, he was released on compassionate grounds and given six months leave of absence. That will take him up until around the 1st of July, when we all know he will be needed at home more even than he is now. Will this whole procedure have to be gone over again? If he does not get a postponement, there will be difficulty then.
There are several young men in training from my constituency who should be at home. Will the same procedure have to be gone through to get their release? What I recommend to the Department of National War Services is that Canada be given a more definite system, a system which will be advertised so that young men can understand
The Address-Mr. Mills

it, and know what action to take if they are key men and it is almost impossible for them to take training. It ought to be arranged so that they will not be trapped, as they are now. The policy should be widely known so that an hon. member is not called upon to intercede for every young farmer in his constituency. That responsibility should not fall upon us. We have enough to do to-day to look after the interests of our constituency, without this extra work.
1 also recommend to the Department of National War Services that a board be set up for every county or constituency, whichever way it would work out best, such board to comprise either two or four men. Where possible, the appointments should be made half from each political group in the riding. In Ontario the executives would be mostly Liberal and Conservative. Such committee would have for its third or fifth member, according to the size agreed upon, a county judge. It would receive applications for postponements, make inquiries, and deal with applications on their merits. The opposition could not then say that this is a Liberal war.
As to the proposed plebiscite, may I say that I have not been favourable to the taking of a plebiscite, and I still wish it could be avoided. But our Prime Minister and cabinet ministers tell us that the matter has been given careful consideration, that the government is unanimously agreed, and that the plebiscite is going to be taken. Therefore there is nothing else to do but to go back to my constituency and advise my electors to go out and vote, making a cross opposite the word "yes", so as to release the government and many private members from pledges previously given the electors respecting the raising of recruits for overseas service. In this way the government would have a free hand to meet the situation which is changing from day to day. This war must be won at any cost or sacrifice.
From my observation during eight years as a member of the house I know that thousands upon thousands of dollars are wasted by every session being prolonged month after month by speeches made for no better reason than that of publicity, so that they may be printed in Hansard and reprinted back home. This is a war session. I know how busy the cabinet is, with the unlimited work connected with the prosecution of the war. Its work is greatly increased while the house is in session, and I should think it would welcome as short a session as possible. I know that help is scarce at home, and most hon. members, including myself, are needed at home.
Therefore I appeal to all private members on this side of the house as well as those in 
opposition groups to refrain from unnecessary, non-constructive speeches. Let us get down to the business of conducting the greatest possible war effort. Let us consider the general business of the country, and conclude this session by May 24, at the latest. This can be done just as well as by staying here until the heat drives us out in July.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the great number of my French-speaking colleagues who have taken part in this debate prompts me to follow their example. Like them, I have always been and still am opposed to conscription for overseas service. I would go further and state that any government attempting to enforce this execrable measure will meet with numerous obstacles and many disappointments in every section of the country. During the last general election campaign of 1940 I made my own the statements coming from my leaders and the electors [DOT]in my constituency, by casting their votes in my favour, ratified the pledges made at the time. I know beforehand that 95 per cent of the electors in my constituency will answer "no" to the question put by the plebiscite and I have no intention of asking them to release me from the solemn pledges I have taken. I therefore intend answering with them in the negative.
For all that, I have not the least objection against the holding of the plebiscite, for it is the fairest method of ascertaining whether or not public opinion has changed in the land, as some claim it has, and it is also the method most in keeping with the democratic principle , of government of the people by the people.
I even believe that the vast majority of the people will answer in the negative and that the effect will be to silence once and for all the voice of those fire-brands and false patriots whose only purpose is self-interest and whose ever readily borrowed cloak of patriotism only serves better to disguise their turpitude and selfishness.
I will therefore vote confidence in the King administration. I will also add a word in connection with the abnormal situation created by calling farmers' sons for military service. Mine is principally an agricultural constituency. More than ever is a greater and more extensive agricultural production being advocated. In order to increase production, cheese factories are being operated over the winter in my constituency; work on the farm is increased as a consequence and this is no time to reduce the number of available farm hands.
The exemption board for the district of Quebec sits in Quebec city, 200 miles from my district. When a farmer's son receives a call

The Address-Mr. Sylvestre
from the registrar, he must within eight days of its receipt send a request for postponement to the latter. The registrar has no authority to decide whether the request should be granted or not, but has to transmit it to the board. The latter sits from time to time and receives hundreds of applications which it hasn't even time to read, with the result that applications for postponement are rejected when they should be granted. On account of the great distance and the consequent expense, farmers and farmers' sons cannot afford to submit their case in person. Because of the serious prejudice resulting therefrom, I would suggest that the board delegate a representative to the districts of Lake St. John and Chicoutimi to meet the applicants, examine their requests on the spot and report to the board.
Otherwise, the way things are going, we are slowly crippling agricultural production which, to my mind, is more necessary to victory than the manufacture of arms and munitions, for, as a consequence of the defeats in the Pacific, there will remain only Canada to supply foodstuffs to Great Britain in the event of the Japanese securing the mastery of the Pacific and cutting communications with New Zealand and Australia.
In addition, lumbering employs thousands of men, and in my district there was a shortage of labour this year. I know that many farmers' sons go to the lumber camps in winter. They are more useful there than in the army, for the work of the woodsman requires a degree of capacity and of physical strength which is not given to all. In calling this class of men to the colours we are crippling another essential industry.
Another serious problem calls for attention on the part of the government. I refer to the movement away from the land. My duties in the army have enabled me to grasp the extent of it for I had occasion to visit many localities, and a continuance of such a situation will spell disaster. A great number of farmers' sons leave the land to work in factories. They are attracted thereto by fairly high salaries, by comparatively short working hours and by the pleasures of city life. Most of them do not save anything, they squander all their earnings and enjoy themselves without any thought for the future. A young man who leaves the farm to work in a factory is lost forever to agriculture and the terrible lesson of the last post-war period is now quite forgotten. As every one knows, one of the main causes of the last depression was the movement away from the land. If nothing is done about this, the next post-war period will be worse than the last one, for when the factories now employing thousands of farmers' sons close their doors, those men will not go
back to the land but will swell the ranks of the unemployed in our large cities, as has happened in the past. The government should make arrangements with the managements of those factories so that inquiries may be made about those who seek employment, and whenever it is found that they are from rural districts, they should not be accepted. Human nature is such that people must sometimes be protected against their own mistakes, but as I say, it is vitally important for our race that farmers' sons should remain at home.
In conclusion, I may say that I cannot understand the reasoning of those who, while claiming that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is our best safeguard, will vote against him. Such is certainly not my way of showing confidence in a man and I feel that in spite of the dark hours at hand and the clouds that are gathering over the horizon, the Prime Minister like the experienced helmsman he is, will bring the ship of state safely into port.
On motion of Mr. Eudes the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Crerar the house adjourned at 10.55 p.m.
